questions.why: The cell theory was proposed by Schleiden and Schwann. Virchow later added that cells come from earlier cells.

questions.q: Osmosis involves movement of
questions.why: Osmosis is the movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane. It is not for gases, proteins or solutes.

questions.q: Bacteria lack
questions.why: Bacteria lack a nuclear membrane, so they have no true nucleus. They do have DNA, ribosomes and a cell membrane.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A red blood cell placed in distilled water bursts. Reason (R): Water enters the cell by osmosis from a hypotonic solution.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Distilled water is hypotonic to the cell, so water enters by osmosis and the red blood cell swells and bursts.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Lysosomes are called suicide bags. Reason (R): Their enzymes can digest the cell's own components when it is damaged.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Lysosomes can digest the cell's own parts if it is damaged, so they are called suicide bags.

questions.q: Which organelle helps detoxify drugs in liver cells?
questions.why: The smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER) helps in detoxifying poisons and drugs, especially in liver cells.

questions.q: Plasmolysis occurs when a plant cell is placed in
questions.why: Plasmolysis occurs when a plant cell is placed in a hypertonic solution, as water leaves the cell and the protoplasm shrinks.

questions.q: Number of daughter cells after one meiosis
questions.why: One meiosis produces four daughter cells, each with half the chromosomes. Mitosis produces two.

questions.q: Case: A student puts one deshelled egg in pure water and another in concentrated salt solution. After 5 hours
questions.why: The egg in pure water gains water by osmosis and swells, while the egg in concentrated salt solution loses water and shrinks.

questions.q: Case: A boiled potato cup with sugar solution in water shows no rise in level. Reason
options: cells are dead, membranes no longer selectively permeable
questions.why: A boiled potato has dead cells, whose membranes are no longer selectively permeable, so osmosis does not occur. So there is no rise in level.

questions.q: Which pair both contain their own DNA and ribosomes?
questions.why: Mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own DNA and ribosomes. The other organelles do not have DNA of their own.

questions.q: If a cell's Golgi apparatus stopped working, the first function to fail would be
questions.why: The Golgi apparatus packages and dispatches proteins and other substances made in the cell. If it failed, this would stop first.

questions.q: A plant cell does not burst in pure water but an animal cell may. The best explanation
options: Plant cell wall resists excess turgor pressure
questions.why: A plant cell has a cell wall that resists the excess pressure (turgor pressure) from water entering. An animal cell has no wall, so it may burst.

courses.title: Ch 6 · Tissues
courses.summary: Why multicellular organisms need tissues, plant meristematic and permanent tissues (simple and complex), and animal epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous tissues.
outcomes: Define tissue and explain why plants and animals have different tissues
Classify meristematic tissues by position and describe their role
Compare parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma, xylem and phloem
Describe the types and functions of epithelial and connective tissues
Compare striated, smooth and cardiac muscle and describe a neuron

scenes.text: Arnav marks a seedling's root tip and the middle of the root with ink dots.
After a few days only the region near the tip has grown longer — that is where dividing tissue lives.

steps.title: What is a tissue?
steps.body: A **tissue** is a group of cells similar in structure and/or working together to perform a particular function (e.g. blood, muscle, xylem). Plants are mostly stationary and need lots of supportive (dead) tissue; growth is limited to certain regions. Animals move, use more energy, and most of their tissues are living; growth is more uniform.

steps.title: Meristematic tissue (plants)
steps.body:
Tissue of actively **dividing cells**, found in growing regions:
- **Apical meristem**: tips of stems and roots — increases **length**.
- **Lateral meristem (cambium)**: increases **girth** (thickness) of stem/root.
- **Intercalary meristem**: at the base of leaves or internodes (on twigs), e.g. in grasses.
Cells: very active, dense cytoplasm, thin cellulose walls, prominent nuclei, **lack vacuoles**.

steps.title: Solved: the onion root experiment
steps.body: Two jars of onions; roots of jar 2 are cut by 1 cm after 2 days. Jar 1 roots keep growing; jar 2 roots stop growing in length, because the **apical meristem** at the tip has been removed.

steps.title: Solved: grass after mowing
steps.body: Grass regrows after mowing because the **intercalary meristem** at the base of leaves keeps dividing.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying meristematic cells have big vacuoles (they lack them — vacuoles would slow division).
- Mixing up apical (length) and lateral (girth).

activity.prompt: Match the meristem with its position/role

quiz.q: Meristematic cells lack
quiz.why: Meristematic cells are dividing cells with dense cytoplasm and a nucleus, but have few or no vacuoles. Vacuoles appear in mature cells.

quiz.q: Girth of a stem increases due to
quiz.why: The lateral meristem (cambium) increases the girth (thickness) of stems and roots. The apical meristem increases length.

quiz.q: A tissue is
options: a group of similar cells doing a function
quiz.why: A tissue is a group of similar cells that together perform a specific function. Many tissues make an organ.

quiz.q: Roots stop growing in length if we cut
quiz.why: The root tip contains the apical meristem, where cells divide to lengthen the root. If cut, the root stops growing in length.

quiz.q: Most plant tissues that support are
quiz.why: Most supportive plant tissues, like sclerenchyma, are dead, since they only give strength. This is why plants can stand up without much energy.

story.title: The coconut husk and the lotus stem

scenes.text: The coconut's husk is tough and fibrous; the lotus stem is full of air spaces and floats.
Both are plant tissues — sclerenchyma for strength, aerenchyma for buoyancy.

steps.title: Simple permanent tissues
steps.body:
Formed when meristematic cells lose the ability to divide (**differentiation**).
- **Parenchyma**: living, thin-walled, loosely packed with intercellular spaces; supports and **stores food**. Variants: **chlorenchyma** (with chlorophyll — photosynthesis), **aerenchyma** (large air cavities — buoyancy in aquatic plants).
- **Collenchyma**: living, elongated, cells irregularly thickened at the corners, little intercellular space; gives **flexibility** (leaf stalks, below the epidermis; lets stems bend without breaking).
- **Sclerenchyma**: **dead**, long and narrow, walls thickened by **lignin**, often no internal space; makes the plant hard and stiff (coconut husk, seed coats, nut shells, veins of leaves, around vascular bundles).

steps.title: Protective tissues
steps.body:
- **Epidermis**: single outer layer; often covered with waxy **cutin** to prevent water loss; in desert plants it is thick. Has **stomata** (pores enclosed by two kidney-shaped **guard cells**) for gas exchange and transpiration. Root epidermis has root hairs for absorption.
- **Cork** (bark of older trees): dead, compactly arranged cells with **suberin** in their walls — impervious to gases and water. Cork from the cork oak is used for bottle stoppers and insulation.

steps.title: Solved: identify the tissue
steps.body: Husk of coconut → sclerenchyma. Leaf stalk bends in the wind → collenchyma. Lotus stem floats → aerenchyma. Green leaf mesophyll → chlorenchyma. Potato stores starch → parenchyma.

steps.title: Solved: functions of stomata
steps.body: Exchange of gases with the atmosphere (CO₂ in, O₂ out in photosynthesis) and **transpiration** — loss of water as vapour, which helps pull water up.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling sclerenchyma living.
- Mixing up cutin (epidermis) and suberin (cork).

activity.prompt: Living or dead at maturity?

quiz.q: Tissue with lignin, dead, giving hardness
quiz.why: Sclerenchyma has thick lignified walls and dead cells, giving hardness and strength. It is found in husk and seed coats.

quiz.q: Aerenchyma helps aquatic plants to
quiz.why: Aerenchyma has large air spaces that help aquatic plants to float. It is a type of parenchyma.

quiz.q: Flexibility to leaf stalks is due to
quiz.why: Collenchyma gives flexibility, which lets leaves and stems bend without breaking. It is found in leaf stalks.

quiz.q: Cork cells contain
quiz.why: Cork cells have a chemical called suberin in their walls, which makes them impermeable to gases and water.

quiz.q: Stomata are enclosed by
quiz.why: Each stoma is enclosed by two guard cells that open and close it. They control gas exchange and water loss.

quiz.q: Food storage in plants is mainly by
quiz.why: Parenchyma cells are thin-walled and living, and they store food. Sclerenchyma and cork are dead.

scenes.text: A tall coconut tree lifts water up from its roots 20 m to its leaves, and sends sugar from leaves down to the roots.
Two separate 'pipes' — xylem and phloem — run side by side as vascular bundles.

steps.title: Xylem
steps.body: Conducts **water and minerals upward** from roots. Elements: **tracheids** and **vessels** (tubular, dead, thick-walled — transport water vertically), **xylem parenchyma** (living — stores food, helps sideways conduction), **xylem fibres** (supportive).

steps.title: Phloem
steps.body: Conducts **food (sugars)** from leaves to other parts — in **both directions**. Elements: **sieve tubes** (tubular cells with perforated walls), **companion cells**, **phloem parenchyma** and **phloem fibres**. All phloem cells are **living except phloem fibres**.

steps.title: Solved: xylem vs phloem
steps.body: Direction: xylem one-way (up); phloem both ways. Material: water + minerals vs food. Living cells: xylem mainly dead (only parenchyma living); phloem mainly living (only fibres dead).

steps.title: Solved: girdling
steps.body: If a ring of bark (including phloem) is removed from a tree trunk, food cannot move down to the roots; the roots eventually starve while water still rises through xylem for a while.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying phloem moves food only downward.
- Saying xylem vessels are living.

activity.prompt: Xylem or phloem?

quiz.q: Water moves up through
quiz.why: Water moves up from the roots to the leaves through the xylem. Phloem carries food.

quiz.q: The only dead element of phloem
quiz.why: Of phloem's elements, only phloem fibres are dead. Sieve tubes, companion cells and parenchyma are living.

quiz.q: The only living element of xylem
quiz.why: Xylem parenchyma is the only living element of xylem. Tracheids, vessels and fibres are dead.

quiz.q: Food moves in phloem
quiz.why: Food moves in the phloem in both directions, up and down, according to the plant's needs. Water in the xylem moves only upwards.

quiz.q: Xylem and phloem are
quiz.why: Xylem and phloem are made of more than one kind of cell working together, so they are complex tissues.

scenes.text: Dhruv fractures his arm; the doctor talks about bone, ligaments, cartilage and blood.
All are connective tissues — different jobs, one family. His skin covering is epithelium.

steps.title: Epithelial tissue
steps.body:
Covering/protective tissue: cells tightly packed in a continuous sheet with little intercellular space, separated from underlying tissue by a **basement membrane**. Controls exchange of materials.
- **Simple squamous**: thin, flat — lining of blood vessels, lung alveoli, mouth/oesophagus lining (thin delicate lining).
- **Stratified squamous**: layers — skin (prevents wear and tear).
- **Columnar** (tall, pillar-like): inner lining of intestine (absorption, secretion); with **cilia** in the respiratory tract (ciliated columnar, moves mucus).
- **Cuboidal**: kidney tubules, ducts of salivary glands (mechanical support).
- **Glandular**: folds inward to form glands that secrete.

steps.title: Connective tissue
steps.body:
Cells loosely spaced in an intercellular **matrix**.
- **Blood**: fluid matrix **plasma** with RBCs, WBCs and platelets; transports gases, food, hormones, wastes.
- **Bone**: hard, strong matrix of **calcium and phosphorus** compounds; framework and support.
- **Ligament**: bone to **bone**; elastic, strong.
- **Tendon**: muscle to **bone**; fibrous, great strength, limited flexibility.
- **Cartilage**: widely spaced cells in a matrix of proteins and sugars; smoothens bone surfaces at joints; in nose, ear, trachea, larynx.
- **Areolar**: between skin and muscles, around blood vessels and nerves, in bone marrow; fills spaces, supports, repairs.
- **Adipose**: below skin and between organs; stores fat, insulates.

steps.title: Solved: identify
steps.body: Lining of kidney tubules → cuboidal epithelium. Muscle attached to bone → tendon. External ear flexibility → cartilage. Fat below skin → adipose. Lining of alveoli → simple squamous.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping ligament (bone–bone) and tendon (muscle–bone).
- Calling blood a 'liquid organ' rather than a connective tissue.

activity.prompt: Match the tissue with where it is found

quiz.q: Muscle is attached to bone by
quiz.why: A tendon joins muscle to bone and is strong and flexible. A ligament connects bone to bone.

quiz.q: The fluid matrix of blood is
quiz.why: The fluid matrix of blood is plasma. It carries cells, nutrients and hormones.

quiz.q: Skin is made of
quiz.why: Skin is made of stratified squamous epithelium, with layers of flat cells to protect against wear. A single layer would wear out.

quiz.q: Bone matrix is rich in
quiz.why: Bone's matrix is hard because it is rich in calcium and phosphorus compounds. Bone is strong and supports the body.

quiz.q: Fat storage tissue
quiz.why: Adipose tissue stores fat, which serves as an energy reserve and insulation. It is found below the skin.

quiz.q: Lining of intestine (absorption)
quiz.why: The intestine lining has columnar epithelium, with tall cells that help in absorption and secretion.

scenes.text: Your heart beats about 70 times a minute, every minute of your life, without tiring.
Cardiac muscle works rhythmically; your arm muscles obey your wishes; nerves carry the messages.

steps.title: Muscular tissue
steps.body:
Elongated **muscle fibres** with **contractile proteins** that contract and relax to cause movement.
- **Striated (skeletal, voluntary)**: long, cylindrical, unbranched, **multinucleate**, light and dark bands (striations); attached to bones; move limbs at will.
- **Smooth (unstriated, involuntary)**: long, spindle-shaped, **uninucleate**; in alimentary canal, iris of eye, ureters, bronchi of lungs; movement of food, etc.
- **Cardiac (involuntary)**: in the heart; cylindrical, **branched**, uninucleate; rhythmic contraction and relaxation throughout life.

steps.title: Nervous tissue
steps.body: Cells of brain, spinal cord and nerves are **neurons**. A neuron has a **cell body** with a nucleus and cytoplasm, short branched **dendrites** (receive messages) and a long **axon** (carries messages; can be up to a metre long). Many nerve fibres bound by connective tissue make a **nerve**. Signals are electrical impulses; nerve and muscle together let us respond quickly.

steps.title: Solved: identify the muscle
steps.body: Biceps → striated. Muscle pushing food in the intestine → smooth. Heart wall → cardiac. Iris adjusting pupil size → smooth.

steps.title: Solved: compare
steps.body: Striated: multinucleate, unbranched, voluntary. Cardiac: uninucleate, branched, involuntary. Smooth: uninucleate, spindle, involuntary.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling cardiac muscle voluntary.
- Saying dendrites carry impulses away from the cell body (the axon does).

activity.prompt: Which muscle type?

quiz.q: Voluntary muscles are
quiz.why: Voluntary muscles (skeletal muscles) are striated, showing light and dark bands. Smooth muscle is not striated.

quiz.q: Cardiac muscle cells are
quiz.why: Cardiac muscle cells are branched and have a single nucleus (uninucleate). They are involuntary and striated.

quiz.q: The long process of a neuron that carries impulses away is the
quiz.why: The axon is the long process of a neuron that carries impulses away from the cell body. Dendrites receive impulses.

quiz.q: Smooth muscle is found in
quiz.why: Smooth muscle is found in the alimentary canal, blood vessels and other organs, where it moves things involuntarily.

quiz.q: A nerve is a bundle of
quiz.why: A nerve is a bundle of nerve fibres (axons) wrapped in connective tissue. It carries signals between the body and the brain.

questions.q: A group of cells performing a common function is a
questions.why: A group of cells with a common function and structure is a tissue. Many tissues form an organ.

questions.q: Apical meristem increases
questions.why: The apical meristem, at the tips of roots and stems, increases their length.

questions.q: Phloem transports
questions.why: The phloem transports food made in the leaves to other parts of the plant. Water is carried by the xylem.

questions.q: Tendon connects
questions.why: A tendon connects muscle to bone. A ligament connects bone to bone.

questions.q: Sclerenchyma cells are
questions.why: Sclerenchyma cells are dead and have thick lignified walls, giving strength and hardness.

questions.q: Neurons are found in
questions.why: Neurons (nerve cells) are found in the brain, spinal cord and nerves. They carry impulses.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Plants have more dead supportive tissue than animals. Reason (R): Plants are stationary and need structural strength.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Plants do not move, so they need much dead supportive tissue for strength.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Cardiac muscles are involuntary. Reason (R): Cardiac muscles are multinucleate and unbranched.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: The assertion is true: cardiac muscles are involuntary. The reason is false, as cardiac muscle cells are uninucleate and branched, not multinucleate and unbranched.

questions.q: Tissue in the husk of coconut
questions.why: The husk of a coconut is made of sclerenchyma, with dead, lignified, long cells that give hardness and strength.

questions.q: Cells of cork have
questions.why: Cork cells have suberin in their walls, which makes them impermeable. They protect the stem.

questions.q: The epithelium lining kidney tubules
questions.why: Kidney tubules are lined by cuboidal epithelium, with cube-shaped cells that help in absorption and secretion. Squamous cells line the lungs.

questions.q: Case: Grass grows back from the base after cutting, but a cut root tip stops growing in length. The tissues involved are
questions.why: Grass regrows from the base because of the intercalary meristem, and a root tip lengthens by its apical meristem. Cutting the tip stops growth in length.

questions.q: Case: A ring of bark is removed from a tree. Which transport is affected first?
questions.why: The phloem lies in the bark. When a ring of bark is removed, food cannot reach the roots from the leaves, so this transport is affected first.

questions.q: Which statement about xylem is correct?
options: Vessels and tracheids are dead and carry water upward
questions.why: The vessels and tracheids of xylem are dead and carry water upwards. Xylem has no companion cells, and phloem carries food.

questions.q: A cell is spindle-shaped, uninucleate and found in the bronchi. Which tissue?
questions.why: Smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped with a single nucleus, and they are found in involuntary organs like the walls of the bronchi. Cardiac muscle is branched and striated muscle is cylindrical.

questions.q: Desert plants have a thick epidermis with cutin mainly to
questions.why: Desert plants have a thick epidermis with a waxy coat of cutin to cut down water loss through evaporation. This helps them survive in dry places.

school-c9-science-b.title: Class 9 Science (Part B)
school-c9-science-b.description: Every chapter of Class 9 Science (NCERT-based) — chemistry, biology and physics: concepts, solved numericals, activities, common mistakes, quizzes and chapter tests, plus revision and mock papers. courses.title: Ch 7 · Motion
courses.summary: Describing motion: distance and displacement, uniform and non-uniform motion, speed and velocity, acceleration, distance–time and velocity–time graphs, the three equations of motion, and uniform circular motion.
outcomes: Distinguish distance from displacement and speed from velocity
Calculate average speed, average velocity and acceleration with units
Draw and interpret distance–time and velocity–time graphs (slope and area)
Derive and apply the three equations of motion
Explain why uniform circular motion is accelerated

scenes.text: Meera runs one full lap of a 400 m track and finishes exactly where she started.
Her coach says: 'You ran 400 m, but your displacement is zero.' How can both be true?

steps.title: Describing position
steps.body: To describe the position of an object we need a **reference point (origin)**. Motion is **relative**: a passenger in a moving bus is at rest relative to the bus but moving relative to the road.

steps.title: Distance vs displacement
steps.body:
- **Distance**: total path length travelled — only magnitude (a **scalar**).
- **Displacement**: shortest distance from initial to final position, **with direction** (a **vector**).
Displacement can be zero even when distance is not. Magnitude of displacement ≤ distance.

steps.title: Uniform and non-uniform motion
steps.body:
- **Uniform motion**: equal distances in equal intervals of time (however small), in a straight line.
- **Non-uniform motion**: unequal distances in equal intervals (a car in traffic).

steps.title: Solved: half a circle
steps.body: A runner goes halfway round a circular track of radius 7 m. Distance = πr = 22/7 × 7 = **22 m**. Displacement = diameter = **14 m** (from start to the opposite point).

steps.title: Solved: walking back
steps.body: Ravi walks 5 m east, then 3 m west. Distance = **8 m**; displacement = **2 m east**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Giving displacement without direction.
- Thinking displacement can be larger than distance.
- Calling a car's motion uniform just because it moves in a straight line.

statements.s: Displacement can be zero when distance is not zero
Distance is a vector
Magnitude of displacement can exceed distance
An object at rest relative to one observer may be moving relative to another

quiz.q: A body completes one full circle. Displacement is
quiz.why: After one full circle the body returns to its starting point, so the straight-line distance between start and end is zero. The distance travelled is 2πr, but displacement is zero.

quiz.q: Displacement is a
quiz.why: Displacement has both magnitude and direction, so it is a vector. Distance and time are scalars.

quiz.q: Walking 4 m north then 3 m east: distance and displacement
quiz.why: The total distance walked is 4 + 3 = 7 m. The displacement is the straight line from start to end: √(4² + 3²) = √25 = 5 m.

quiz.q: Equal distances in equal time intervals in a straight line is
quiz.why: Equal distances in equal time intervals, along a straight line, means constant speed, which is uniform motion. Unequal distances would be non-uniform motion.

quiz.q: SI unit of displacement
quiz.why: Displacement is a length, so its SI unit is the metre (m). m/s is for speed and m/s² for acceleration.

scenes.text: The school bus covers 18 km in 30 minutes but stops at many signals.
Its speedometer swings between 0 and 60 km/h. What single number describes the trip? Average speed.

steps.title: Speed
steps.body:
**Speed** = distance travelled per unit time. SI unit **m/s** (also km/h).
**Average speed** = total distance ÷ total time.
Conversion: **1 km/h = 5/18 m/s**; 1 m/s = 3.6 km/h.

steps.title: Velocity
steps.body:
**Velocity** = speed in a definite direction = displacement per unit time. Changes if speed **or** direction changes.
For uniformly changing velocity in a straight line, **average velocity = (u + v)/2**, where u is initial and v final velocity.

steps.title: Solved: the round trip trap
steps.body: Go 60 km at 30 km/h (2 h), return 60 km at 60 km/h (1 h). Average speed = 120 km / 3 h = **40 km/h** (not 45!). Average velocity = 0 (back at start).

steps.title: Solved: average velocity
steps.body: A car's velocity changes uniformly from 18 km/h (5 m/s) to 36 km/h (10 m/s). Average velocity = (5 + 10)/2 = **7.5 m/s**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Averaging speeds for equal distances (use total distance ÷ total time).
- Forgetting to convert km/h to m/s before using SI formulas.

activity.prompt: Convert 72 km/h to m/s

quiz.q: 1 km/h equals
quiz.why: 1 km/h = 1000 m ÷ 3600 s = 5/18 m/s. To convert km/h to m/s, multiply by 5/18.

quiz.q: Car travels 150 km in 3 h: average speed
quiz.why: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time = 150 ÷ 3 = 50 km/h.

quiz.q: Velocity changes when
quiz.why: Velocity has both speed and direction, so it changes if either of them changes. A car going round a bend at constant speed still changes velocity.

quiz.q: 10 m/s in km/h
quiz.why: To convert m/s to km/h, multiply by 18/5: 10 × 3.6 = 36 km/h.

quiz.q: A sprinter runs 100 m in 10 s: speed
quiz.why: Speed = distance ÷ time = 100 ÷ 10 = 10 m/s.

quiz.q: Velocity uniformly from 2 m/s to 8 m/s: average velocity
quiz.why: For uniform acceleration the average velocity = (u + v)/2 = (2 + 8)/2 = 5 m/s.

scenes.text: When the signal turns green, a scooter goes from 0 to 10 m/s in 5 s.
Its velocity increased by 2 m/s every second — an acceleration of 2 m/s².

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
**Acceleration a = change in velocity ÷ time = (v − u)/t**. SI unit **m/s²** (m s⁻²).
- Positive acceleration: velocity increasing in its direction.
- Negative acceleration (**retardation/deceleration**): velocity decreasing.
- **Uniform acceleration**: velocity changes by equal amounts in equal time intervals (freely falling body). Non-uniform: unequal changes (car in traffic).

steps.title: Solved: braking
steps.body: A train at 90 km/h (25 m/s) stops in 50 s. a = (0 − 25)/50 = **−0.5 m/s²** (retardation 0.5 m/s²).

steps.title: Solved: bicycle downhill
steps.body: Rahul's bicycle speeds up downhill from 3 m/s to 18 m/s in 10 s. a = (18 − 3)/10 = **1.5 m/s²**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing units as m/s (velocity) instead of m/s².
- Ignoring the sign: deceleration means a is negative.

activity.prompt: A car accelerates from 4 m/s to 24 m/s in 5 s. Acceleration?

quiz.q: SI unit of acceleration
quiz.why: Acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time, so its unit is (m/s) ÷ s = m/s².

quiz.q: A body moving with constant velocity has acceleration
quiz.why: Constant velocity means no change in speed or direction, so acceleration is zero.

quiz.q: Velocity drops from 20 m/s to 10 m/s in 5 s: a =
quiz.why: a = (v − u)/t = (10 − 20)/5 = −2 m/s². The negative sign shows slowing down (retardation).

quiz.q: A freely falling body has
quiz.why: A freely falling body speeds up by about 9.8 m/s every second, which is uniform acceleration due to gravity. Its velocity is not constant.

quiz.q: Retardation means
quiz.why: Retardation (deceleration) means negative acceleration, in which the velocity of the body decreases.

scenes.text: A TV analyst shows a graph of a bowler's run-up speed against time.
The slope shows how fast he speeds up; the area under it shows how far he ran.

steps.title: Distance–time graph
steps.body:
- **Uniform speed**: straight line; **slope = speed**. Steeper line = faster.
- **At rest**: horizontal line.
- **Non-uniform speed**: curved line.
Speed = (s₂ − s₁)/(t₂ − t₁).

steps.title: Velocity–time graph
steps.body:
- **Slope = acceleration**.
- **Area under the graph = displacement** (distance in straight-line motion without reversal).
- Horizontal line: uniform velocity (a = 0).
- Straight sloping line: uniform acceleration.
- Curve: non-uniform acceleration.

steps.title: Solved: area under v–t
steps.body: A car moves at a steady 40 km/h for 2 h: the v–t graph is horizontal; area = 40 × 2 = **80 km** (a rectangle).

steps.title: Solved: uniform acceleration
steps.body: v–t line from 0 m/s at t = 0 to 20 m/s at t = 10 s. Slope = 2 m/s². Area (triangle) = ½ × 10 × 20 = **100 m**.

steps.title: Solved: trapezium area
steps.body: Velocity rises uniformly from 5 m/s to 15 m/s in 4 s. Distance = area of trapezium = ½(5 + 15) × 4 = **40 m**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading distance from a v–t graph as the y-value (use the area).
- Confusing slope of s–t (speed) with slope of v–t (acceleration).

activity.prompt: What does each graph show?

quiz.q: Slope of a distance–time graph gives
quiz.why: The slope of a distance-time graph is distance ÷ time, which is speed. A steeper line means higher speed.

quiz.q: Area under a velocity–time graph gives
quiz.why: The area under a velocity-time graph equals the displacement (distance for straight-line motion). The slope gives acceleration.

quiz.q: A v–t graph parallel to the time axis means
quiz.why: A v-t line parallel to the time axis means velocity is constant, so the acceleration is zero.

quiz.q: v–t: 0 to 30 m/s in 6 s. Acceleration
quiz.why: a = (30 − 0)/6 = 5 m/s², the slope of the v-t graph.

quiz.q: Same graph: distance in 6 s
quiz.why: Distance = area under the graph = area of the triangle = ½ × 6 × 30 = 90 m.

quiz.q: A horizontal s–t graph means the object is
quiz.why: A horizontal line on a distance-time graph means the distance is not changing, so the object is at rest.

lessons.title: Equations of motion and circular motion

scenes.text: A driving instructor asks: at 72 km/h, if brakes give −5 m/s², how far will the car go before stopping?
Without a measuring tape, the third equation of motion gives the answer: 40 m.

steps.title: The three equations (uniform acceleration, straight line)
steps.body:
1. **v = u + at** (velocity–time)
2. **s = ut + ½at²** (position–time)
3. **2as = v² − u²** (position–velocity)
Graphical derivation: on a v–t graph from u to v in time t, slope a = (v − u)/t gives (1); area of trapezium = ½(u + v)t = ut + ½at² gives (2); eliminating t gives (3).

steps.title: Solved: train from rest
steps.body: A train starts from rest, a = 0.5 m/s² for 2 min (120 s). v = 0 + 0.5 × 120 = **60 m/s**; s = ½ × 0.5 × 120² = **3600 m**.

steps.title: Solved: stone thrown up (a = −10 m/s²)
steps.body: u = 20 m/s upward. At top v = 0: height = u²/(2g) = 400/20 = **20 m**; time to top = 2 s.

steps.title: Uniform circular motion
steps.body: Motion along a circle at constant **speed**. The **direction** changes at every point, so velocity changes ⇒ it is **accelerated motion**. Speed v = **2πr/t** for one revolution in time t. Examples: the Moon around the Earth, an athlete on a circular track, a stone whirled on a thread (released, it flies off **tangentially**).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the equations when acceleration is not uniform.
- Mixing units (km/h with m/s²).
- Saying uniform circular motion has zero acceleration.

activity.prompt: A ball starts from rest with a = 2 m/s². Distance covered in 5 s?

quiz.q: v = u + at gives
quiz.why: v = u + at gives the final velocity v after time t, given initial velocity u and acceleration a.

quiz.q: A car at 10 m/s accelerates at 2 m/s² for 3 s. v =
From rest, a = 4 m/s², distance after 3 s
quiz.why: From rest, s = ½at² = ½ × 4 × 3² = ½ × 4 × 9 = 18 m.

quiz.q: Uniform circular motion is accelerated because
quiz.why: In uniform circular motion, the speed is constant but the direction keeps changing. A changing velocity means acceleration, so the motion is accelerated.

quiz.q: A satellite orbit radius 42250 km, period 24 h. Its speed is about
quiz.why: Speed = circumference ÷ period = 2π × 42250 ÷ 24 ≈ 11,061 km/h, about 3.07 km/s. The satellite goes round once in 24 hours.

quiz.q: A stone whirled in a circle, when released, moves
quiz.why: When released, the stone flies off along the tangent to the circle at that point, as it keeps the direction of its velocity at that instant.

questions.q: SI unit of speed
questions.why: Speed is distance per unit time, so its SI unit is m/s. m/s² is the unit of acceleration.

questions.q: Displacement after one full round of a circle
questions.why: After one full round the body is back at its start, so the displacement is zero. The distance is 2πr.

questions.q: Slope of a velocity–time graph gives
questions.why: The slope of a velocity-time graph = change in velocity ÷ time, which is acceleration.

questions.q: 54 km/h in m/s
A car goes from 0 to 20 m/s in 4 s. Acceleration
Distance covered at 15 m/s for 1 minute
questions.why: 1 minute = 60 s, so distance = speed × time = 15 × 60 = 900 m.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Uniform circular motion is accelerated. Reason (R): Direction of velocity changes continuously.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. In uniform circular motion the direction of velocity changes continuously, so the velocity changes, which means acceleration.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Average speed for going 10 km at 20 km/h and returning at 30 km/h is 25 km/h. Reason (R): Average speed = total distance/total time.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: The assertion is false: the average speed is total distance ÷ total time = 20 ÷ (0.5 + 1/3) = 24 km/h, not the simple mean 25. The reason is true.

questions.q: A bus decreases speed from 80 km/h to 60 km/h in 5 s. Acceleration ≈
questions.why: The change is −20 km/h = −5.56 m/s, so a = −5.56 ÷ 5 ≈ −1.11 m/s². The negative sign shows the bus is slowing down.

questions.q: Area under v–t: velocity rises 0 → 12 m/s in 6 s, then constant for 4 s. Total distance
questions.why: The distance is the area under the graph. For the first 6 s, ½ × 6 × 12 = 36 m. For the next 4 s at 12 m/s: 12 × 4 = 48 m. Total = 84 m.

questions.q: A trolley going down an incline from rest has a = 2 cm/s². Velocity after 3 s
Case: A driver sees a child 50 m ahead while moving at 20 m/s and brakes with −5 m/s² (no reaction delay). The car
questions.why: With v² = u² + 2as: 0 = 400 − 2 × 5 × s, so s = 400 ÷ 10 = 40 m. That is less than 50 m, so the car stops safely.

questions.q: Case: Same car but the driver reacts after 0.5 s before braking. Total stopping distance
questions.why: During the 0.5 s reaction time the car moves at 20 m/s for 10 m, then needs 40 m to stop. Total = 10 + 40 = 50 m.

questions.q: A stone is thrown up at 15 m/s (g = 10 m/s²). Maximum height
An athlete runs a circular track of diameter 200 m in 40 s. Displacement after 2 min 20 s
questions.why: 2 min 20 s = 140 s, which is 140/40 = 3.5 rounds. After half a round, the athlete is at the opposite point, so the displacement is the diameter, 200 m.

questions.q: Distance in the nth second for a body from rest with acceleration a is
questions.why: The distance in the nth second = s(n) − s(n − 1) = ½a[n² − (n − 1)²] = ½a(2n − 1) = a(2n − 1)/2.

courses.title: Ch 8 · Force and Laws of Motion
courses.summary: Balanced and unbalanced forces, Newton's three laws, inertia and mass, momentum and F = ma, impulse, action–reaction pairs and conservation of momentum, with everyday applications.
outcomes: Distinguish balanced and unbalanced forces and their effects
State Newton's first law and relate inertia to mass
Define momentum and use F = ma = Δp/t
Identify action–reaction pairs (third law)
Apply conservation of momentum to collisions and recoil

lessons.title: Balanced and unbalanced forces; the first law

scenes.text: A magician pulls a tablecloth out quickly — the plates stay on the table!
Plates 'want' to stay at rest. That tendency is inertia, described by Newton's first law.

steps.title: Force
steps.body:
A **force** is a push or pull. It can change an object's **speed**, its **direction** of motion, or its **shape**. SI unit: **newton (N)**.
- **Balanced forces**: net force zero — no change in the state of rest or uniform motion (may change shape).
- **Unbalanced forces**: net force non-zero — cause **acceleration**. Friction usually opposes motion.

steps.title: Newton's first law (law of inertia)
steps.body:
**An object remains in a state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless compelled to change that state by an applied (unbalanced) force.** Galileo's inclined-plane reasoning first suggested this: without friction a ball would roll on forever.
**Inertia**: the natural tendency to resist a change in state of rest or motion. **Mass is the measure of inertia** — heavier objects have more inertia.

steps.title: Solved: the bus jerk
steps.body: A bus starts suddenly — passengers fall **backward** (their bodies tend to stay at rest). It brakes suddenly — they fall **forward** (bodies tend to keep moving). Seat belts counter this.

steps.title: Solved: carom coin
steps.body: Strike the bottom coin of a stack sharply: it flies out while the others drop straight down — the upper coins' inertia of rest.

steps.title: Solved: dusting a carpet
steps.body: Beating a carpet sets it moving; dust particles, due to inertia of rest, stay behind and fall off.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying a force is needed to keep a body moving at constant velocity (only to overcome friction).
- Saying inertia depends on speed (it depends on mass).

statements.s: A body moving at constant velocity has zero net force on it
A heavier stone has more inertia than a lighter one
Passengers fall backward when a bus brakes
Balanced forces can change an object's shape
Inertia depends on the speed of the object

quiz.q: Mass is a measure of
quiz.why: Mass is a measure of inertia, the resistance of a body to a change in its motion. A larger mass means greater inertia.

quiz.q: When a bus starts suddenly, passengers fall
quiz.why: When the bus starts suddenly, the passengers' bodies tend to stay at rest because of inertia, while the bus moves forward. So they fall backward.

quiz.q: Unbalanced forces produce
quiz.why: An unbalanced force changes the velocity of a body, so it produces acceleration. Balanced forces cause no change.

quiz.q: Which has more inertia?
quiz.why: A train has the greatest mass among these, so it has the most inertia. A feather has little.

quiz.q: SI unit of force
quiz.why: The SI unit of force is the newton (N). Joule is for energy, watt for power and pascal for pressure.

quiz.q: The first law is also called the law of
quiz.why: Newton's first law states that a body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by an unbalanced force. It is called the law of inertia.

scenes.text: A fielder pulls his hands back while catching a fast ball.
By taking more time to stop it, he reduces the force on his palms — Newton's second law in action.

steps.title: Momentum
steps.body: **Momentum p = m × v**, a vector in the direction of velocity. SI unit **kg m/s**. A slow truck and a fast bullet can both have large momentum.

steps.title: Second law
steps.body:
**The rate of change of momentum is directly proportional to the applied unbalanced force, in the direction of the force.**
F ∝ (mv − mu)/t = m(v − u)/t = **ma**. With SI units, **F = ma**. **1 N** = force that gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s² (1 kg m s⁻²).
**Impulse** = F × t = change in momentum. Increasing the stopping time reduces the force.

steps.title: Solved: force from acceleration
steps.body: A 1500 kg car is accelerated at 1.7 m/s². F = ma = 1500 × 1.7 = **2550 N**.

steps.title: Solved: stopping a car
steps.body: A 1000 kg car at 72 km/h (20 m/s) stops in 4 s. a = −5 m/s²; F = 1000 × (−5) = **−5000 N** (braking force 5000 N opposite to motion).

steps.title: Solved: bullet
steps.body: A 20 g bullet moving at 150 m/s is stopped by a constant force in 0.03 s. Δp = 0.02 × 150 = 3 kg m/s ⇒ F = 3/0.03 = **100 N**.

steps.title: Everyday applications
steps.body: High-jumpers land on foam beds; athletes in long jump land on sand; cars have crumple zones and airbags; fielders draw hands back — all increase the time of impact and so reduce force.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using grams instead of kilograms.
- Forgetting momentum's direction (velocity sign).
- Saying a force is needed for constant momentum.

activity.prompt: Force needed to give a 5 kg mass an acceleration of 4 m/s²

quiz.q: Momentum =
quiz.why: Momentum is the product of mass and velocity, p = m × v. It is a vector.

quiz.q: SI unit of momentum
quiz.why: Momentum = mass × velocity, so its unit is kg × m/s = kg m/s.

quiz.q: A fielder lowers his hands to
options: increase the time and reduce force
quiz.why: By lowering his hands, the fielder increases the time over which the ball stops. The change in momentum is the same, so the force is smaller, and the catch hurts less.
1 newton is the force that gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s², so 1 N = 1 kg m/s².

quiz.q: F = 10 N on 2 kg: acceleration
Momentum of a 2 kg ball at 3 m/s
quiz.why: Momentum = mass × velocity = 2 × 3 = 6 kg m/s.

scenes.text: Sunil pushes water backward with his oar, and the boat moves forward.
Every push gets an equal push back — that's Newton's third law.

steps.title: Statement
steps.body: **When one object exerts a force on another, the second exerts a force on the first that is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.** These **action–reaction** forces act on **different objects**, at the same instant, so they never cancel each other.

steps.title: Solved: examples
steps.body:
- Walking: foot pushes the ground backward; ground pushes the foot forward.
- Gun recoil: gun pushes bullet forward; bullet pushes gun backward.
- Rocket: pushes exhaust gases backward; gases push the rocket forward.
- A sailor jumping forward from a boat pushes the boat backward.

steps.title: Solved: why don't they cancel?
steps.body: Horse pulls a cart: the cart pulls back equally on the horse. They don't cancel because they act on different bodies. The horse–cart system moves because the **ground pushes the horse forward** (friction) more than friction holds the cart back.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying action and reaction cancel (they act on different objects).
- Saying the reaction comes after the action (they are simultaneous).

statements.s: Action and reaction act on the same body
Action and reaction are equal and opposite
A rocket moves forward because exhaust gases push it
Action and reaction cancel each other

quiz.q: When you push a wall, the wall
quiz.why: By Newton's third law, when you push the wall, the wall pushes you back with an equal force in the opposite direction.

quiz.q: Gun recoil is explained by the
quiz.why: When the bullet is fired forward, the gun gets an equal and opposite push backward. This recoil is explained by Newton's third law.

quiz.q: Action and reaction forces act
quiz.why: Action and reaction forces are equal and opposite but act on different bodies, so they do not cancel.

quiz.q: A swimmer moves forward by
quiz.why: A swimmer pushes the water backward, and the water pushes the swimmer forward by the third law. This moves the swimmer ahead.

quiz.q: Walking is possible because the ground
quiz.why: We push the ground backward with our foot, and the ground pushes our foot forward. This reaction lets us walk.

scenes.text: Two skaters stand still on ice, then push each other apart.
The lighter one zooms off faster. Total momentum before = 0 = total momentum after.

steps.title: Law
steps.body:
**When no external unbalanced force acts, the total momentum of a system is conserved.** For two objects A and B colliding:
m_A u_A + m_B u_B = m_A v_A + m_B v_B.
(From the third law: F_AB = −F_BA during the same time t, so the momentum gained by one equals the momentum lost by the other.)

steps.title: Solved: gun recoil
steps.body:
A 4 kg gun fires a 50 g bullet at 35 m/s. Initial momentum 0.
0 = 0.05 × 35 + 4 × v ⇒ v = −1.75/4 = **−0.4375 m/s** (gun recoils backward at about 0.44 m/s).

steps.title: Solved: girl jumps onto cart
steps.body: A 40 kg girl running at 5 m/s jumps onto a 3 kg stationary cart. 40 × 5 = (40 + 3)v ⇒ **v ≈ 4.65 m/s**.

steps.title: Solved: hockey players
steps.body: Hockey player A (60 kg, 5 m/s) collides with player B (55 kg, at rest) and they move together: v = 300/115 ≈ **2.61 m/s** in A's direction.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting signs for opposite directions.
- Using conservation when a large external force (e.g. friction) acts strongly.

activity.prompt: A 2 kg ball at 3 m/s hits a stationary 1 kg ball and they stick together. Common velocity?

quiz.q: Total momentum is conserved when
quiz.why: The total momentum of a system is conserved when no external unbalanced force acts on it. External forces could change it.

quiz.q: A gun recoils because
quiz.why: Before firing, the total momentum is zero. After firing, the bullet's momentum forward is balanced by the gun's momentum backward, so momentum is conserved.

quiz.q: A 1 kg ball at 10 m/s hits a 4 kg stationary ball and sticks. v =
quiz.why: Momentum before = 1 × 10 = 10. After sticking, (1 + 4) × v = 10, so v = 2 m/s.

quiz.q: Before firing, a gun–bullet system's momentum is
quiz.why: Before firing, both the gun and the bullet are at rest, so the total momentum is zero.

quiz.q: Recoil velocity of a gun is small because
quiz.why: Gun and bullet have equal and opposite momentum, and the gun has a much larger mass. So its recoil velocity is much smaller than the bullet's.

questions.q: A force can change an object's
questions.why: A force can change the speed, direction or shape of an object. It can't change its mass.

questions.q: Newton's first law defines
questions.why: Newton's first law defines inertia, as the tendency of a body to resist a change in its state of rest or motion.

questions.q: SI unit of force
questions.why: The SI unit of force is the newton (N), named after Isaac Newton.

questions.q: Action and reaction act on
questions.why: Action and reaction forces always act on different objects. If they were on the same object, they would cancel.

questions.q: F = 25 N, m = 5 kg: acceleration
Momentum of a 0.5 kg ball at 20 m/s
questions.why: Momentum = 0.5 × 20 = 10 kg m/s.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A cricketer draws his hands back while catching. Reason (R): It increases the time, reducing the force for the same change in momentum.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Drawing the hands back increases the time of stopping, so the force is smaller for the same change in momentum.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Action and reaction cancel each other. Reason (R): They are equal and opposite.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: The assertion is false because action and reaction act on different bodies, so they cannot cancel each other. The reason is true: they are equal and opposite.

questions.q: A 1200 kg car accelerates from 10 m/s to 20 m/s in 5 s. Force
A 10 g bullet at 400 m/s embeds in a block and stops in 0.02 s. Average force
questions.why: Change in momentum = 0.01 × 400 = 4 kg m/s. Force = 4 ÷ 0.02 = 200 N.

questions.q: Change in momentum of a 2 kg ball whose velocity changes from 5 m/s to −5 m/s (it bounces back)
questions.why: Change in momentum = m(v − u) = 2(−5 − 5) = −20 kg m/s. Its magnitude is 20 kg m/s.

questions.q: Case: A 50 kg boy jumps from a stationary 100 kg boat forward at 2 m/s. Boat's velocity
questions.why: Total momentum is zero: 50 × 2 + 100 × v = 0, so v = −1 m/s. The boat moves 1 m/s backward.

questions.q: Case: An 8000 kg engine pulls 5 wagons of 2000 kg each with force 40000 N; friction 5000 N. Acceleration of the train
In the same train, the force of wagon 1 on wagon 2 (wagons 2–5 behind it, friction ignored per wagon)
questions.why: Wagons 2-5 have a mass of 4 × 2000 = 8000 kg, and need a force of 8000 × 1.944 ≈ 15,556 N from wagon 1.

questions.q: Two 100 g objects move toward each other at 2 m/s and 1 m/s. After colliding, the first moves back at 0.67 m/s. The second then moves (in the first object's original direction) at
questions.why: Total momentum is conserved: 0.1 × 2 − 0.1 × 1 = 0.1 kg m/s. After: 0.1(−0.67) + 0.1v = 0.1, so v = 1.67 m/s.

courses.title: Ch 9 · Gravitation
courses.summary: Newton's universal law of gravitation, free fall and g, mass vs weight (Earth and Moon), thrust and pressure, buoyancy, Archimedes' principle and relative density.
outcomes: State and apply the universal law of gravitation, F = Gm₁m₂/d²
Derive g = GM/R² and solve free-fall problems
Distinguish mass from weight and compare weight on the Moon
Calculate pressure as thrust per unit area
Explain buoyancy and floating/sinking using Archimedes' principle and density
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition; relative density may be trimmed in rationalised editions

scenes.text: Legend says a falling apple made Isaac Newton wonder: if Earth pulls an apple, does it pull the Moon too?
It does. The same force that drops the apple keeps the Moon in its orbit.

steps.title: The law
steps.body:
**Every object in the universe attracts every other object with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them**, along the line joining their centres:
**F = G m₁m₂ / d²**
**G** = universal gravitation constant = **6.673 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²** (measured by Henry Cavendish). The force is always attractive and acts even across empty space.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.body: It explains: the force binding us to Earth; the motion of the Moon around the Earth; planets around the Sun; **tides** due to the Moon and Sun. (Kepler's third law — the cube of a planet's mean distance from the Sun is proportional to the square of its orbital period, r³ ∝ T² — helped Newton arrive at the inverse-square law.)

steps.title: Solved: changing distance
steps.body: If the distance between two masses is **halved**, F becomes 2² = **4 times**. If tripled, F becomes 1/9. If one mass is doubled, F doubles.

steps.title: Solved: why don't we feel it between people?
steps.body: Two 50 kg students 1 m apart: F = 6.7 × 10⁻¹¹ × 2500 / 1 ≈ 1.7 × 10⁻⁷ N — far too small to notice. Gravity becomes important only when at least one mass is huge (planet, star).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using d instead of d² (inverse **square**).
- Thinking the Moon doesn't fall — it is falling toward Earth all the time, but its sideways speed keeps it in orbit.
- Saying Earth attracts the apple more than the apple attracts Earth (forces are equal; Earth's acceleration is tiny because its mass is huge).

activity.label: Distance between two masses (as a multiple of the original)

quiz.q: Value of G (SI)
quiz.why: The universal gravitational constant G = 6.673 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². The other values are the speed of light, Earth's mass and g.

quiz.q: Distance doubled ⇒ gravitational force
quiz.why: Gravitational force is inversely proportional to the square of the distance. If distance doubles, the force becomes 1/2² = one-fourth.

quiz.q: Tides are caused mainly by
quiz.why: Tides are mainly caused by the Moon's gravitational pull on the oceans. The Sun also has a smaller effect.

quiz.q: Earth pulls an apple with force F. The apple pulls Earth with
quiz.why: By Newton's third law, the apple pulls the Earth with an equal force F in the opposite direction. The Earth's acceleration is tiny due to its huge mass.

quiz.q: Both masses doubled, distance same ⇒ force
quiz.why: F is proportional to the product of the masses, so doubling both gives 2 × 2 = 4 times the force.

lessons.title: Free fall and acceleration due to gravity

scenes.text: On Earth a coin falls faster than a feather.
Astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather on the Moon in 1971 — they landed together. No air, no difference.

steps.title: Free fall
steps.body:
Objects falling only under Earth's gravity are in **free fall**. All objects have the same acceleration **g** regardless of mass (if air resistance is negligible).
From F = mg and F = GMm/R²: **g = GM/R²**. With M = 6 × 10²⁴ kg, R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m: g ≈ **9.8 m/s²**.
Earth is not a perfect sphere — its radius is larger at the equator — so **g is greater at the poles** than at the equator. g also decreases with height.

steps.title: Equations with g
steps.body:
Use the equations of motion with a = g (taking downward as positive for falling objects, or a = −g for upward throws):
v = u + gt, s = ut + ½gt², v² = u² + 2gs.

steps.title: Solved: car off a cliff
steps.body: A car falls off a ledge and hits the ground in 0.5 s (g = 10 m/s²). v = 0 + 10 × 0.5 = **5 m/s**; height = ½ × 10 × 0.25 = **1.25 m**; average speed = 2.5 m/s.

steps.title: Solved: ball thrown up
steps.body: Thrown up to 10 m (g = 9.8 m/s²): u² = 2gh = 196 ⇒ **u = 14 m/s**; time to top = 14/9.8 ≈ **1.43 s**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking heavier objects fall faster in vacuum.
- Mixing the sign of g when the object goes up.
- Confusing g (9.8 m/s², changes with place) with G (universal constant).

activity.prompt: A stone is dropped from rest. Speed after 3 s? (g = 9.8 m/s²)

quiz.q: g on Earth's surface is about
quiz.why: The acceleration due to gravity on Earth's surface is about 9.8 m/s².

quiz.q: g =
quiz.why: g = GM/R², where M and R are the mass and radius of the Earth. Substituting F = GMm/R² and F = mg gives this.

quiz.q: g is greater at
quiz.why: g is greater at the poles, because the Earth is slightly flattened there, so the poles are nearer the centre. It is smaller at the equator and on mountain tops.

quiz.q: In vacuum, a feather and a coin dropped together
quiz.why: In a vacuum there is no air resistance, so all bodies fall with the same acceleration. A feather and a coin land together.

quiz.q: A ball thrown up at 20 m/s (g = 10) reaches height
quiz.why: At the top v = 0: h = u²/2g = 400/20 = 20 m.

quiz.q: G is
quiz.why: G is a universal constant. It has the same value everywhere, unlike g.

scenes.text: An astronaut weighing 600 N on Earth bounces around on the Moon.
Her mass is still 61 kg, but her weight is only about 100 N there.

steps.title: Mass vs weight
steps.body:
- **Mass**: amount of matter; measure of inertia; **same everywhere**; SI unit kg; a scalar; measured with a beam balance.
- **Weight**: force with which a body is attracted to Earth (or another body): **W = mg**; SI unit **newton**; a vector acting downward; changes with g; measured with a spring balance.

steps.title: Weight on the Moon
steps.body: Moon's mass and radius are smaller, so its surface gravity is about **1/6** of Earth's. **Weight on Moon ≈ (1/6) × weight on Earth.** (Moon: M ≈ 7.36 × 10²² kg, R ≈ 1.74 × 10⁶ m.)

steps.title: Solved: on Earth and the Moon
steps.body: Mass 10 kg: weight on Earth = 10 × 9.8 = **98 N**; on the Moon = 98/6 ≈ **16.3 N**. Mass is 10 kg in both places.

steps.title: Solved: from weight
steps.body: An object weighs 10 N on Earth. Its weight on the Moon = **1.67 N**; its mass = 10/9.8 ≈ **1.02 kg**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying 'my weight is 50 kg' — that's mass; weight would be about 490 N.
- Thinking mass changes on the Moon.

activity.prompt: Mass or weight?

quiz.q: Weight of a 5 kg bag (g = 9.8)
quiz.why: Weight = mg = 5 × 9.8 = 49 N.

quiz.q: Weight on the Moon is about
quiz.why: The Moon's gravity is about one-sixth of Earth's, so a body weighs about 1/6 as much there.

quiz.q: Mass of a body on the Moon compared to Earth
quiz.why: Mass is the amount of matter in a body and does not depend on place. So it is the same on the Moon.

quiz.q: Weight is measured with a
quiz.why: Weight is a force, measured with a spring balance. A beam balance compares masses.

quiz.q: Earth weight 120 N ⇒ Moon weight
quiz.why: The weight on the Moon is 1/6 of that on Earth: 120 ÷ 6 = 20 N.

scenes.text: A camel walks easily on desert sand while a person in high heels sinks.
Same type of force — weight — spread over a large area makes less pressure.

steps.title: Thrust and pressure
steps.body:
**Thrust**: the net force acting perpendicular to a surface (unit N).
**Pressure = thrust ÷ area** (P = F/A). SI unit **pascal (Pa) = N/m²**.
Same force on a smaller area → **greater pressure**: sharp knives cut better; nails have pointed tips; school bags have broad straps; buildings have wide foundations; tanks and trucks have broad tyres/tracks.

steps.title: Pressure in fluids
steps.body: Liquids and gases exert pressure in **all directions** and on the walls of their containers. Pressure in a liquid increases with depth.

steps.title: Solved: the wooden block
steps.body:
A 5 kg block 40 cm × 20 cm × 10 cm (g = 9.8 m/s²); weight 49 N.
On the 20 cm × 10 cm face (0.02 m²): P = 49/0.02 = **2450 Pa**.
On the 40 cm × 20 cm face (0.08 m²): P = 49/0.08 = **612.5 Pa**.

steps.title: Solved: drawing pin
steps.body: Thumb pushes a pin with 10 N; tip area 0.1 mm² = 1 × 10⁻⁷ m². P = 10/10⁻⁷ = **10⁸ Pa** — huge, so it enters wood easily.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to convert cm² to m² (1 cm² = 10⁻⁴ m²).
- Saying a bigger area increases pressure.

activity.prompt: A 60 kg person stands on two feet of total area 0.03 m² (g = 10). Pressure?

quiz.q: SI unit of pressure
quiz.why: The SI unit of pressure is the pascal (Pa), equal to 1 N/m².

quiz.q: Broad straps on a school bag
quiz.why: Broad straps spread the weight over a larger area, which lowers the pressure on the shoulders.

quiz.q: Pressure =
quiz.why: Pressure is the thrust (force) acting on a unit area: pressure = thrust ÷ area.

quiz.q: A knife cuts better when sharp because
quiz.why: A sharp knife has a very small edge area, so the same force produces a much greater pressure. That cuts more easily.

quiz.q: 1 Pa =
quiz.why: 1 pascal is a pressure of 1 newton per square metre: 1 Pa = 1 N/m².

scenes.text: Pulling a full bucket up a well feels easy until it leaves the water.
Water pushes up on objects in it — the same push lets a giant steel ship float.

steps.title: Buoyancy
steps.body: A fluid exerts an **upward force (upthrust/buoyant force)** on an object immersed in it. An object **floats** if its density is **less** than the liquid's; it **sinks** if its density is **greater**. (A cork floats, an iron nail sinks.)

steps.title: Archimedes' principle
steps.body: **When a body is immersed fully or partially in a fluid, it experiences an upward force equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by it.** Uses: designing ships and submarines; **lactometers** (purity of milk) and **hydrometers** (density of liquids).

steps.title: Density and relative density
steps.body: **Density** = mass/volume (kg/m³). **Relative density** = density of a substance ÷ density of water (no unit). Density of water = 1000 kg/m³.

steps.title: Solved: relative density
steps.body: Density of a substance 5000 kg/m³ ⇒ RD = 5000/1000 = **5**. Silver's RD is 10.8 ⇒ density = **10 800 kg/m³**.

steps.title: Solved: float or sink?
steps.body: A 500 g packet with volume 350 cm³: density = 500/350 ≈ 1.43 g/cm³ > 1 ⇒ **sinks** in water. Mass of water displaced = 350 g.

steps.title: Solved: apparent loss of weight
steps.body: A stone weighs 6 N in air and 4 N in water. Upthrust = **2 N** = weight of water displaced ⇒ volume ≈ 2/(1000 × 9.8) ≈ 2.04 × 10⁻⁴ m³.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying heavy objects always sink (a ship floats — density matters, including the air inside).
- Saying upthrust equals the object's weight in every case (only when floating).

activity.prompt: Float or sink in water (density 1 g/cm³)?

quiz.q: Upthrust equals the weight of
quiz.why: By Archimedes' principle, the upthrust on a body in a fluid equals the weight of the fluid it displaces.

quiz.q: Relative density has
quiz.why: Relative density is a ratio of two densities, so it has no unit.

quiz.q: An object floats if its density is
quiz.why: An object floats if its density is less than that of the liquid. A denser object sinks.

quiz.q: Purity of milk is tested with a
quiz.why: A lactometer measures the density of milk and so tests its purity. A hydrometer measures the density of liquids in general.

quiz.q: Stone 10 N in air, 7 N in water: upthrust
quiz.why: Upthrust = weight in air − weight in water = 10 − 7 = 3 N.

quiz.q: RD of a substance with density 2700 kg/m³
quiz.why: Relative density = density of substance ÷ density of water = 2700 ÷ 1000 = 2.7.

questions.q: The law of gravitation was given by
questions.why: Isaac Newton gave the universal law of gravitation. Kepler studied planetary motion and Einstein gave general relativity.

questions.q: SI unit of weight
questions.why: Weight is a force, so its SI unit is the newton (N). The kilogram is the unit of mass.

questions.q: Weight on the Moon compared with Earth
questions.why: The Moon's gravity is about one-sixth of Earth's, so weight there is about one-sixth.

questions.q: Pressure = thrust /
questions.why: Pressure = thrust ÷ area. A larger area gives less pressure.

questions.q: A ball dropped from rest falls for 2 s (g = 10). Speed
Force between two masses when distance is tripled
questions.why: Force is inversely proportional to the square of the distance. If the distance triples, F becomes F/3² = F/9.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A heavy and a light stone dropped together in vacuum reach the ground together. Reason (R): Acceleration due to gravity is independent of the mass of the falling body.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. In a vacuum, g does not depend on mass, so both stones fall with the same acceleration and land together.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A sharp knife cuts better than a blunt one. Reason (R): For the same force, smaller area gives greater pressure.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. A sharp knife has a smaller edge area, so the same force gives greater pressure.

questions.q: Mass 60 kg on Earth; weight on the Moon (g = 9.8)
questions.why: The weight on Earth = 60 × 9.8 = 588 N. On the Moon it is about 1/6 of that: 588 ÷ 6 = 98 N.

questions.q: A stone thrown up at 19.6 m/s. Time to return to the thrower (g = 9.8)
questions.why: The time of flight = 2u/g = 2 × 19.6 ÷ 9.8 = 4 s. It goes up for 2 s and comes down for 2 s.

questions.q: A 1 kg object of volume 500 cm³ in water (density 1 g/cm³) will
questions.why: Density = 1000 g ÷ 500 cm³ = 2 g/cm³, which is more than water's 1 g/cm³. So it sinks.

questions.q: Case: A brick 20 cm × 10 cm × 5 cm of mass 2 kg (g = 10). Maximum pressure it can exert on the floor
questions.why: Pressure is greatest on the smallest face: 10 cm × 5 cm = 0.005 m². Weight = 2 × 10 = 20 N, so P = 20 ÷ 0.005 = 4000 Pa.

questions.q: Case: An astronaut's spring balance reads 600 N on Earth. On a planet with twice Earth's mass and twice its radius, it reads
questions.why: g' = G(2M)/(2R)² = G·2M/4R² = g/2. So the weight is half of 600 N, which is 300 N.

questions.q: Using g = GM/R² with M = 6 × 10²⁴ kg, R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m, G = 6.7 × 10⁻¹¹: g ≈
A stone of weight 15 N in air weighs 10 N fully immersed in water. Its relative density
questions.why: Loss of weight in water (upthrust) = 15 − 10 = 5 N. Relative density = weight in air ÷ loss of weight = 15 ÷ 5 = 3.

questions.q: Why does a ball dropped from a tall building hit the ground at a much lower speed than the free-fall calculation predicts?
options: g is larger at the top
questions.why: Air resistance opposes the motion of a falling ball and grows with speed. So it reaches the ground at a lower speed than the free-fall calculation, which ignores air.

courses.title: Ch 10 · Work and Energy
courses.summary: Scientific meaning of work, positive/negative/zero work, kinetic and potential energy, the law of conservation of energy, power, and the commercial unit kilowatt hour.
outcomes: Calculate work done by a constant force, including negative and zero work
Derive and use KE = ½mv² and PE = mgh
Apply conservation of energy to falling bodies and energy transformations
Calculate power and convert kWh to joules

scenes.text: Aman pushes a wall for ten minutes until he sweats. 'I did so much work!'
His physics teacher smiles: 'The wall didn't move — scientifically, you did zero work on it.'

steps.title: Scientific meaning of work
steps.body:
Work is done when (1) a **force acts** on an object and (2) the object is **displaced** (in the direction of the force or against it).
**W = F × s** (force × displacement along the force). Work is a scalar. SI unit: **joule (J)**; 1 J = work done when a force of 1 N displaces an object by 1 m along the force.

steps.title: Positive, negative and zero work
steps.body:
- **Positive**: force and displacement in the same direction (pulling a toy car forward).
- **Negative**: force opposite to displacement — W = −F × s (friction on a sliding box; brakes; gravity on a ball going up).
- **Zero**: no displacement (pushing a wall) or force ⟂ displacement (a porter carrying a load on his head horizontally does no work against gravity).

steps.title: Solved: work
steps.body:
A force of 5 N moves an object 2 m along the force: W = 5 × 2 = **10 J**.
A 7 N force moves a cart 8 m: **56 J**.

steps.title: Solved: lifting
steps.body: Lifting a 2 kg bag 1.5 m up (g = 10): F = 20 N, W = 20 × 1.5 = **30 J**. Gravity does −30 J on it.

steps.title: Solved: negative work
steps.body: A sliding block covers 4 m while friction of 3 N acts on it. Work by friction = **−12 J**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling 'effort' work without displacement.
- Forgetting the negative sign when force opposes motion.
- Multiplying force by distance perpendicular to the force.

activity.prompt: Positive, negative or zero work by the stated force?

items.text: You pull a bucket up from a well (your force)
Gravity on a ball thrown upward (going up)
Porter's upward force while walking horizontally

quiz.q: SI unit of work
quiz.why: The SI unit of work is the joule (J), equal to 1 newton × 1 metre.

quiz.q: Work done when F = 10 N moves a body 3 m along F
quiz.why: Work = force × displacement = 10 × 3 = 30 J, as the force is along the motion.

quiz.q: Work is zero when
options: force and displacement are along the same line
quiz.why: Work = F s cos θ, which is zero when the force is perpendicular to the displacement, as cos 90° = 0.

quiz.q: Work done by friction on a moving object is usually
quiz.why: Friction acts opposite to the motion, so the work it does is negative. It takes energy away from the moving object.

quiz.q: Work is a
quiz.why: Work has magnitude but no direction, so it is a scalar quantity. It can be positive, negative or zero.

scenes.text: A moving hammer drives a nail; a stretched bow shoots an arrow.
The hammer has energy because it moves; the bow because of its changed shape. Energy is the capacity to do work.

steps.title: Energy
steps.body: **Energy** is the capacity of doing work; SI unit **joule** (1 kJ = 1000 J). Forms: kinetic, potential, heat, chemical, electrical, light, sound, nuclear.

steps.title: Kinetic energy
steps.body: Energy possessed by an object due to its **motion**. Work done to accelerate a mass m from rest to v: W = F × s = ma × (v²/2a) = **½mv²**. Hence **KE = ½mv²**. Doubling v makes KE four times.

steps.title: Potential energy
steps.body: Energy stored due to **position or configuration** (stretched rubber band, wound spring, raised object). Gravitational PE of mass m at height h: work done against gravity = mg × h ⇒ **PE = mgh**. It depends on the vertical height, **not on the path** taken.

steps.title: Solved: work to speed up a car
Solved: PE
steps.body: 10 kg raised 6 m (g = 9.8): PE = 10 × 9.8 × 6 = **588 J**. A 12 kg object at a height where PE = 480 J (g = 10) ⇒ h = 480/120 = **4 m**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to square v.
- Using path length instead of vertical height for PE.
- Using km/h directly in ½mv².

activity.prompt: Kinetic energy of a 2 kg ball moving at 5 m/s

quiz.q: KE =
quiz.why: Kinetic energy is ½mv², the energy a body has due to its motion. mgh is potential energy.

quiz.q: If speed doubles, KE becomes
quiz.why: KE is proportional to v², so doubling the speed makes KE 2² = 4 times.

quiz.q: PE of 2 kg at 5 m (g = 10)
A wound spring of a toy car has
quiz.why: A wound spring stores energy because of its changed shape, which is elastic potential energy. The car moves when it unwinds.

quiz.q: PE depends on
quiz.why: Potential energy depends on the vertical height, not on the path taken. mgh uses only the height.

quiz.q: Mass 4 kg moving with KE 50 J. Speed
quiz.why: ½ × 4 × v² = 50, so 2v² = 50, v² = 25 and v = 5 m/s.

scenes.text: Grandfather's clock pendulum swings up, pauses, swings down — again and again.
At the top it is all potential energy; at the bottom, mostly kinetic. Energy changes form but the total stays (almost) the same.

steps.title: Law of conservation of energy
steps.body:
**Energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be transformed from one form to another.** The total energy before and after a transformation remains the same.
For a freely falling body (no air resistance): **PE + KE = constant** (mechanical energy): mgh + ½mv² = constant.

steps.title: Solved: falling object table (m = 20 kg, h = 4 m, g = 10)
steps.body:
h = 4 m: PE 800 J, KE 0, total 800 J
h = 3 m: PE 600 J, KE 200 J
h = 2 m: PE 400 J, KE 400 J
h = 1 m: PE 200 J, KE 600 J
just above ground: PE 0, KE 800 J — total always **800 J**.

steps.title: Solved: speed at the bottom
steps.body: A ball dropped from 5 m (g = 10): mgh = ½mv² ⇒ v = √(2gh) = √100 = **10 m/s** — independent of mass.

steps.title: Transformations around us
steps.body:
- Green plants: light → chemical (photosynthesis).
- Hydroelectric dam: PE of water → KE → electrical.
- Burning fuel: chemical → heat and light.
- Electric fan: electrical → kinetic; bulb: electrical → light + heat.
- Battery: chemical → electrical.
- Sun: nuclear → heat and light.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying energy 'disappears' when a ball stops — it becomes heat and sound (friction).
- Assuming KE = PE always; it is the **sum** that stays constant.

activity.prompt: Match the device with its main energy change

quiz.q: Energy can be
quiz.why: Energy can be transformed from one form to another, but cannot be created or destroyed. This is the law of conservation of energy.

quiz.q: A freely falling ball halfway down has
quiz.why: A ball dropped from rest has total energy mgh. Halfway down, half of its PE has become KE, so PE and KE are equal.

quiz.q: Speed of an object dropped from 20 m just before impact (g = 10)
quiz.why: All of the PE turns to KE: mgh = ½mv², so v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 10 × 20) = √400 = 20 m/s.

quiz.q: Energy change in a solar panel
quiz.why: A solar panel converts light energy into electrical energy. It does not convert heat into light.

quiz.q: At the highest point of a pendulum swing, energy is mostly
quiz.why: At the highest point of a swing, the pendulum is momentarily at rest, so its energy is mostly potential.

scenes.text: Two girls of the same weight climb the same rope; one takes 20 s, the other 50 s.
They do the same work but at different rates — different power.

steps.title: Power
steps.body: **Power = rate of doing work = W/t**. SI unit **watt (W)**: 1 W = 1 J/s. 1 kW = 1000 W. **Average power** = total energy ÷ total time.

steps.title: Commercial unit of energy
steps.body: **1 kilowatt hour (kWh)** = energy used in 1 hour at a rate of 1 kW = 1000 W × 3600 s = **3.6 × 10⁶ J**. Electricity bills count 'units' — 1 unit = 1 kWh.

steps.title: Solved: a boy on stairs
steps.body: A 50 kg boy runs up 45 steps of 15 cm each in 9 s (g = 10). h = 6.75 m; W = 50 × 10 × 6.75 = 3375 J; P = 3375/9 = **375 W**.

steps.title: Solved: electricity bill
steps.body: A 60 W bulb runs 6 h a day for 30 days: energy = 0.06 kW × 6 h × 30 = **10.8 kWh** (units) = 10.8 × 3.6 × 10⁶ J ≈ 3.89 × 10⁷ J. At ₹7 per unit, cost ≈ ₹75.6.

steps.title: Solved: home usage
steps.body: 250 units in a month = 250 kWh = 250 × 3.6 × 10⁶ = **9 × 10⁸ J**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing kW (power) and kWh (energy).
- Forgetting to convert minutes to seconds (or hours for kWh).

activity.prompt: An electric heater of 1500 W runs for 2 hours. Energy used in kWh?

quiz.q: SI unit of power
quiz.why: The SI unit of power is the watt (W), equal to 1 joule per second. Joule is the unit of energy.

quiz.q: 1 kWh equals
A motor does 6000 J in 1 minute. Power
quiz.why: Power = work ÷ time = 6000 ÷ 60 = 100 W.

quiz.q: A 100 W bulb for 10 h uses
quiz.why: Energy = power × time = 0.1 kW × 10 h = 1 kWh.

quiz.q: Power =
quiz.why: Power is the rate of doing work, so P = W/t. A larger power does the same work in less time.

quiz.q: 1 unit on an electricity bill =
quiz.why: One 'unit' of electricity on the bill is 1 kilowatt-hour (kWh), the energy used by a 1 kW device in one hour.

questions.q: SI unit of energy
questions.why: The SI unit of energy is the joule (J). Watt is for power.

questions.q: Work done when no displacement occurs
questions.why: Work = force × displacement. If there is no displacement, the work done is zero.

questions.q: KE of a body at rest
questions.why: KE = ½mv². At rest v = 0, so the kinetic energy is zero.

questions.q: 1 kW =
questions.why: 1 kilowatt = 1000 watts.

questions.q: A 20 N force moves a box 5 m along the force. Work
questions.why: Work = force × displacement = 20 × 5 = 100 J.

questions.q: PE of 3 kg at 10 m (g = 9.8)
Assertion (A): A porter carrying a load on his head and walking on level ground does no work against gravity. Reason (R): The displacement is perpendicular to the force of gravity.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. The force of gravity acts vertically, and the porter moves horizontally, so the displacement is perpendicular to the force and the work done is zero.

questions.q: Assertion (A): When speed doubles, KE doubles. Reason (R): KE = ½mv².
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: The assertion is false: KE = ½mv² is proportional to v², so doubling the speed makes KE 4 times. The reason is true.

questions.q: A 40 kg girl climbs 5 m stairs in 10 s (g = 10). Power
Mass 1 kg falls from 10 m (g = 10). KE just before hitting the ground
questions.why: All the PE becomes KE just before landing: mgh = 1 × 10 × 10 = 100 J.

questions.q: Work needed to stop a 1000 kg car moving at 20 m/s
questions.why: Work needed = the KE to be removed = ½mv² = ½ × 1000 × 400 = 2 × 10⁵ J.

questions.q: Case: A family uses a 1 kW heater 2 h/day, four 50 W bulbs 5 h/day for 30 days. Energy used
questions.why: Heater: 1 kW × 2 h = 2 kWh. Bulbs: 4 × 0.05 kW × 5 h = 1 kWh. Per day 3 kWh, so for 30 days 3 × 30 = 90 kWh.

questions.q: Case: A 5 kg ball is dropped from 10 m (g = 10). At 4 m above the ground, its KE
questions.why: At 4 m above the ground, the ball has fallen 6 m. KE = loss of PE = mg × 6 = 5 × 10 × 6 = 300 J.

questions.why: v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 10 × 45) = √900 = 30 m/s. The mass does not matter.
