A pump lifts 1000 kg of water to 20 m in 50 s (g = 10). Power

courses.title: Ch 11 · Sound
courses.summary: Production and propagation of sound as a longitudinal wave, wavelength, frequency, amplitude and speed, reflection, echo and reverberation, the range of hearing, ultrasound, SONAR and the human ear.
outcomes: Explain how sound is produced by vibration and needs a medium
Describe compressions and rarefactions and use v = λν and T = 1/ν
Relate pitch to frequency and loudness to amplitude
Calculate echo distances and SONAR depths
List uses of ultrasound and describe how we hear

scenes.text: In a lab, an electric bell rings inside a glass jar. The air is slowly pumped out.
The ringing grows fainter and fainter though the hammer still strikes — sound needs a medium.

steps.title: Production
steps.body: Sound is produced by **vibrating objects** — a stretched string, a tuning fork, our **vocal cords**, a drum membrane, the wings of a bee. A vibrating tuning fork touched to water makes splashes; touched to a hanging ping-pong ball, it kicks the ball away.

steps.title: Propagation
steps.body:
Sound needs a **material medium** (solid, liquid or gas) and **cannot travel through vacuum**. A vibrating object pushes neighbouring particles, creating regions of high pressure/density — **compressions (C)** — and low pressure/density — **rarefactions (R)**. The disturbance travels; the particles only oscillate about their positions.
Sound is a **longitudinal wave**: particles vibrate **parallel** to the direction of propagation. (In **transverse** waves, like ripples on water or light, particles vibrate **perpendicular** to it.)

steps.title: Solved: why is the Moon silent?
steps.body: There is no air on the Moon, so astronauts talk using radios (radio waves are electromagnetic and travel through vacuum).

steps.title: Solved: Slinky model
steps.body: Push and pull one end of a stretched Slinky along its length: compressions and rarefactions travel along it — a model of a longitudinal (sound) wave. Moving the end up and down instead makes a transverse wave.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying sound can travel in vacuum.
- Saying air particles travel from the source to your ear (only the disturbance travels).

statements.s: Sound can travel through vacuum
Sound waves in air are longitudinal
Compressions are regions of low pressure
Our voice is produced by vibrating vocal cords
Light is a longitudinal wave

quiz.q: Sound is produced by
quiz.why: Sound is produced when objects vibrate. Without vibration, there is no sound.

quiz.q: Sound cannot travel through
quiz.why: Sound needs a medium to travel, so it cannot pass through a vacuum. It travels through water, air and steel.

quiz.q: In a longitudinal wave, particles vibrate
quiz.why: In a longitudinal wave, the particles vibrate parallel (back and forth) to the direction in which the wave travels. Sound is such a wave.

quiz.q: Regions of low density in a sound wave are
quiz.why: In a sound wave, regions where the particles are spread out, with low density, are rarefactions. Compressions have high density.

quiz.q: Bell-jar experiment proves sound needs
quiz.why: When air is pumped out of the bell jar, the sound of the bell fades. This shows sound needs a medium.

scenes.text: At a school concert a flute plays high notes and a big drum booms low.
On an oscilloscope, the flute's wave is crowded and the drum's is spread out — different frequencies.

steps.title: Terms
steps.body:
- **Wavelength λ**: distance between two consecutive compressions (or rarefactions); unit m.
- **Frequency ν**: number of oscillations (compressions passing a point) per second; unit **hertz (Hz)**.
- **Time period T**: time for one oscillation; **T = 1/ν**.
- **Amplitude A**: maximum disturbance (pressure/density variation) from the mean value.
- **Speed v = λν** (distance travelled by a compression per unit time).

steps.title: What we hear
steps.body:
- **Pitch** depends on **frequency**: higher frequency → higher pitch (shrill). A woman's voice is usually higher-pitched than a man's.
- **Loudness** depends on **amplitude** (energy): larger amplitude → louder. Loudness is measured in decibels (dB).
- **Quality (timbre)** lets us distinguish two sounds of the same pitch and loudness (a violin vs a flute). A sound of a single frequency is a **tone**; a mixture is a **note**; pleasant sound is music, unpleasant is noise.
- **Intensity**: sound energy per second through unit area.

steps.title: Solved: wavelength
steps.body: A 220 Hz note in air at 330 m/s: λ = v/ν = 330/220 = **1.5 m**. Time period = 1/220 ≈ 0.0045 s.

steps.title: Solved: speed from a wave
steps.body: A wave of frequency 2 kHz has wavelength 35 cm: v = 2000 × 0.35 = **700 m/s**.

steps.title: Solved: oscillations
steps.body: A source makes 40 oscillations in 0.2 s ⇒ ν = 200 Hz, T = **0.005 s**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up pitch (frequency) and loudness (amplitude).
- Using cm with m/s without converting.

activity.prompt: Speed of sound 340 m/s and frequency 170 Hz. Wavelength?

quiz.q: Pitch depends on
quiz.why: Pitch depends on frequency: the higher the frequency, the higher the pitch. Amplitude decides loudness.

quiz.q: Loudness depends on
quiz.why: Loudness depends on the amplitude of the vibration. A larger amplitude gives a louder sound.

quiz.q: v =
quiz.why: The wave speed is the product of wavelength and frequency: v = λν.

quiz.q: Frequency 500 Hz ⇒ time period
quiz.why: Time period = 1 ÷ frequency = 1/500 = 0.002 s.

quiz.q: SI unit of frequency
quiz.why: Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz), the number of vibrations per second.

quiz.q: Two sounds with the same pitch and loudness are distinguished by
quiz.why: Two sounds with the same pitch and loudness can still differ in their quality, or timbre. It lets us tell instruments apart.

lessons.title: Speed of sound, reflection, echo and reverberation

scenes.text: During a storm, Sana sees lightning and counts 3 seconds before the thunder.
Light arrives almost instantly; sound at about 344 m/s — so the lightning was about 1 km away.

steps.title: Speed in different media
steps.body:
Sound is fastest in solids, slower in liquids, slowest in gases; it increases with temperature. Approximate values: air 331 m/s (0 °C), **344 m/s (22 °C)**; distilled water ~1498 m/s; sea water ~1531 m/s; iron/steel ~5950 m/s; aluminium ~6420 m/s.
Objects faster than sound (supersonic jets) create **shock waves** heard as a **sonic boom**.

steps.title: Reflection and echo
steps.body:
Sound reflects from hard surfaces obeying the laws of reflection (angle of incidence = angle of reflection; incident ray, reflected ray and normal in the same plane).
**Echo**: a reflected sound heard distinctly. The sensation of sound persists in our brain about **0.1 s**, so the echo must return after ≥ 0.1 s. At 344 m/s the total path ≥ 34.4 m ⇒ the reflector must be at least **17.2 m** away.
**Reverberation**: persistence of sound due to repeated reflections in a big hall; reduced by sound-absorbing materials (fibreboard, rough plaster, curtains, seat materials).

steps.title: Uses of multiple reflection
steps.body: Megaphones, horns, trumpets and shehnais (sound directed forward); the **stethoscope** (doctor hears heartbeat via multiple reflections in the tube); **curved ceilings** of concert halls and **soundboards** behind the stage spread sound evenly.

steps.title: Solved: thunder
steps.body: Delay 3 s at 344 m/s: distance ≈ 344 × 3 = **1032 m ≈ 1 km**.

steps.title: Solved: echo from a cliff
steps.body: A shout echoes back after 3 s; speed 342 m/s. Distance to cliff = (342 × 3)/2 = **513 m** (sound goes there and back).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to halve the distance in echo problems.
- Saying sound is faster in air than in water.

activity.prompt: A person hears an echo 2 s after clapping. Speed of sound 340 m/s. Distance of the wall?

quiz.q: Sound travels fastest in
quiz.why: Sound travels fastest in solids, as the particles are closest together. So it travels fastest in steel, then water, then air.

quiz.q: Minimum distance for a distinct echo (v = 344 m/s)
quiz.why: For a distinct echo, the sound must return after at least 0.1 s. The distance covered = 344 × 0.1 = 34.4 m, so the reflector must be at 17.2 m.

quiz.q: Reverberation is reduced by
quiz.why: Reverberation is reduced by sound-absorbing materials, such as curtains, carpets and panels. They reduce repeated reflections.

quiz.q: A stethoscope works on
quiz.why: A stethoscope works on multiple reflection of sound, as the sound from the chest travels along the tube to the doctor's ears.

quiz.q: Echo heard after 4 s, v = 330 m/s: distance of reflector
quiz.why: The sound travels to the reflector and back in 4 s, so total distance = 330 × 4 = 1320 m, and the reflector is 1320 ÷ 2 = 660 m away.

quiz.q: Sonic boom is produced by
quiz.why: A sonic boom is a shock wave produced by objects moving faster than the speed of sound, such as supersonic jets.

lessons.title: Range of hearing, ultrasound, SONAR and the human ear

scenes.text: Bats fly at night without bumping into anything.
They emit high-pitched ultrasonic squeaks and listen for echoes — nature's SONAR.

steps.title: Audible range
steps.body: Humans hear about **20 Hz to 20 000 Hz (20 kHz)**. Children under 5 and some animals (dogs) hear up to 25 kHz. Below 20 Hz is **infrasound** (rhinoceroses communicate around 5 Hz; whales and elephants use infrasound; some animals sense infrasound before earthquakes). Above 20 kHz is **ultrasound** (dolphins, bats, porpoises use it; rats can produce it).

steps.title: Uses of ultrasound
steps.body:
- Cleaning hard-to-reach parts (spiral tubes, odd-shaped parts, electronic components) in a cleaning solution.
- Detecting cracks and flaws in metal blocks.
- **Echocardiography** — images of the heart.
- **Ultrasonography** — images of internal organs (liver, gall bladder, uterus, kidney) and of a foetus.
- Breaking small kidney stones into fine grains.

steps.title: SONAR
steps.body: **SO**und **N**avigation **A**nd **R**anging uses ultrasound to measure distance, direction and speed of underwater objects. A transmitter sends ultrasound; a detector receives the echo. **Distance d = (v × t)/2**. Used for sea depth, locating submarines, shipwrecks, icebergs, underwater hills and valleys.

steps.title: Solved: depth of the sea
steps.body: Ultrasound echo returns after 3.42 s; speed in sea water 1531 m/s. d = 1531 × 3.42 / 2 ≈ **2618 m**.

steps.title: How we hear
steps.body:
- **Outer ear**: the **pinna** collects sound; it travels through the **auditory canal**.
- The **eardrum (tympanic membrane)** vibrates with compressions and rarefactions.
- **Middle ear**: three tiny bones — **hammer, anvil and stirrup** — amplify the vibrations.
- **Inner ear**: the **cochlea** converts pressure variations into electrical signals sent by the **auditory nerve** to the brain.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying ultrasound is louder sound (it is higher-frequency sound).
- Forgetting to halve the SONAR time.
- Saying humans hear infrasound.

activity.prompt: Infrasound, audible or ultrasound?

quiz.q: Human audible range
quiz.why: The human audible range is 20 Hz to 20 kHz. Below it is infrasound and above it is ultrasound.

quiz.q: SONAR uses
quiz.why: SONAR uses ultrasound waves to find the depth of the sea and locate objects. The waves are reflected back.

quiz.q: The three bones of the middle ear amplify
quiz.why: The three small bones of the middle ear amplify the vibrations received from the eardrum. They pass them to the inner ear.

quiz.q: Pressure variations are converted into electrical signals in the
quiz.why: The cochlea of the inner ear converts the pressure variations into electrical signals, which go to the brain through the auditory nerve.

quiz.q: SONAR echo after 2 s in water at 1500 m/s: depth
quiz.why: The sound travels to the sea bed and back: total distance = 1500 × 2 = 3000 m. Depth = 3000/2 = 1500 m.

quiz.q: Images of the heart using ultrasound
quiz.why: Imaging the heart with ultrasound is called echocardiography. X-rays or MRI use other waves.

questions.q: Sound is a
questions.why: Sound is a longitudinal wave, as the particles of the medium vibrate along the direction of travel. It is not an electromagnetic wave.

questions.q: Unit of frequency
questions.why: Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz). Decibel is the unit of loudness.

questions.q: Frequencies above 20 kHz are
questions.why: Sound above 20 kHz is above the human audible range, so it is ultrasonic. Infrasonic is below 20 Hz.

questions.q: Loudness depends on
questions.why: Loudness depends on amplitude. Wavelength and frequency are not the cause.

questions.q: Wave with v = 330 m/s and λ = 0.66 m has frequency
Frequency 100 Hz: time period
questions.why: Time period = 1 ÷ frequency = 1/100 = 0.01 s.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Sound cannot travel on the Moon's surface. Reason (R): There is no atmosphere (air) on the Moon.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. The Moon has no atmosphere to carry sound, so sound cannot travel there.

questions.q: Assertion (A): An echo is heard only if the reflector is at least 17.2 m away (v = 344 m/s). Reason (R): Sensation of sound persists in the brain for about 0.1 s.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. The sound sensation lasts about 0.1 s in the brain, and sound travels 34.4 m in that time. So the reflector must be at least 17.2 m away.

questions.q: Thunder heard 5 s after lightning (v = 340 m/s). Distance of the lightning
questions.why: Light reaches us almost instantly, so the sound time is 5 s. Distance = speed × time = 340 × 5 = 1700 m.

questions.q: A shout into an 85 m deep dry well echoes from the bottom (v = 340 m/s). The echo returns after
questions.why: Total distance = 2 × 85 = 170 m. Time = 170 ÷ 340 = 0.5 s.

questions.q: Case: In a large hall, speech sounds blurred because of repeated reflections. The engineer should
questions.why: Absorbing panels and curtains reduce the repeated reflections that cause reverberation. A bigger hall or glass walls would make it worse.

questions.q: Case: A ship's SONAR gets an echo from the sea bed after 4 s. Speed in sea water 1531 m/s. Depth
questions.why: Distance to the bed = (speed × time) ÷ 2 = 1531 × 4 ÷ 2 = 3062 m.

questions.q: A sound wave travels 1.5 km in 1.25 s. Its speed in m/s is
questions.why: Speed = distance ÷ time = 1500 ÷ 1.25 = 1200 m/s.

questions.q: Which change makes a sound louder and higher-pitched?
questions.why: A louder sound has a larger amplitude, and a higher pitch has a higher frequency. So both need to change together.

questions.q: A person claps near a cliff and hears the echo after 2 s. He walks 85 m toward the cliff. New echo time (v = 340 m/s)
questions.why: The echo in 2 s means the cliff is 340 × 2 ÷ 2 = 340 m away. After walking 85 m, the distance is 255 m, so the echo time is 2 × 255 ÷ 340 = 1.5 s.

questions.q: Frequency of a source is doubled in the same medium. Wavelength becomes
questions.why: The speed of sound in a medium is fixed. Since λ = v/ν, doubling the frequency halves the wavelength.

courses.title: Ch 12 · Improvement in Food Resources
courses.summary: How India feeds its people: crop variety improvement, crop production management (nutrients, manure, fertilisers, irrigation, cropping patterns), crop protection and storage, plus animal husbandry, fisheries and bee-keeping.
outcomes: Explain why and how crop varieties are improved (hybridisation, GM crops) and the desirable traits
Name kharif and rabi crops and their seasons
List the 16 plant nutrients and compare manure with fertilisers
Compare irrigation methods and mixed cropping, intercropping and crop rotation
Describe crop protection, grain storage and the basics of cattle, poultry, fish and bee farming
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition; animal husbandry may be trimmed in rationalised editions (kept as an extension)

lessons.title: Food, crops and crop variety improvement

scenes.text: India must feed more than 140 crore people while farmland is limited.
After the Green Revolution (grains) and White Revolution (milk), the next aim is sustainable, nutritious food for all — starting with better crop varieties.

steps.title: Crops and seasons
steps.body:
- Cereals (wheat, rice, maize, millets, sorghum) — carbohydrates.
- Pulses (gram, pea, black gram, green gram, pigeon pea, lentil) — proteins.
- Oilseeds (soybean, groundnut, sesame, castor, mustard, linseed, sunflower) — fats.
- Vegetables, spices, fruits — vitamins and minerals; fodder crops (berseem, oats, Sudan grass) for livestock.
**Kharif crops** grow in the rainy season (**June to October**): paddy, soybean, pigeon pea, maize, cotton, green gram, black gram.
**Rabi crops** grow in winter (**November to April**): wheat, gram, peas, mustard, linseed.
Crops need specific temperature, photoperiod (day length) and water.

steps.title: Crop variety improvement
steps.body:
Breeding for useful traits:
- **Hybridisation**: crossing genetically dissimilar plants — intervarietal (between varieties), interspecific (between species of the same genus), intergeneric (between genera).
- **Genetic modification**: introducing a gene for a desired trait → **GM crops**.
Varieties are tested, and good-quality seeds of the same variety are produced for farmers.

steps.title: Desired traits
steps.body:
- **Higher yield** per acre.
- **Improved quality**: baking quality in wheat, protein in pulses, oil quality in oilseeds, preserving quality in fruits/vegetables.
- **Biotic and abiotic resistance**: to diseases, insects, nematodes and to drought, salinity, waterlogging, heat, cold, frost.
- **Change in maturity duration**: shorter duration lets farmers grow more crops a year and lowers cost.
- **Wider adaptability**: one variety for many regions.
- **Desirable agronomic traits**: tallness and profuse branching in fodder crops; dwarfness in cereals (less nutrient use).

steps.title: Solved: kharif or rabi?
steps.body: Paddy, cotton, maize, soybean → kharif. Wheat, gram, mustard, peas → rabi.

steps.title: Solved: which trait matters?
steps.body: A farmer in a drought-prone district → drought tolerance (abiotic resistance). A dairy farmer growing fodder → tall, profusely branched variety. A biscuit factory → wheat with good baking quality.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying kharif crops grow in winter.
- Thinking hybridisation and GM crops are the same (GM involves inserting a gene).

activity.prompt: Kharif or rabi crop?

quiz.q: Kharif crops are grown in
quiz.why: Kharif crops are sown with the onset of the rainy season, in June-July, and harvested in October. Examples are paddy and soybean.

quiz.q: Which is a rabi crop?
quiz.why: Wheat is a rabi crop, sown in winter (November) and harvested in spring. Paddy, soybean and cotton are kharif crops.

quiz.q: Pulses are a rich source of
quiz.why: Pulses are a rich source of proteins, while cereals give carbohydrates and oilseeds give fats.

quiz.q: Crossing two different species of the same genus is
quiz.why: Crossing between two different species of the same genus is called interspecific hybridisation. Crossing different genera is intergeneric.

quiz.q: Dwarfness is desirable in
quiz.why: Dwarfness is desirable in cereals, as it needs less nutrition and avoids lodging (falling over). Fodder crops need tall plants.

quiz.q: A crop with a gene inserted for a desired trait is
quiz.why: A crop in which a gene for a desired trait has been introduced is a genetically modified (GM) crop. It is not a simple hybrid.

scenes.text: Farmer Kamla's wheat leaves turn pale yellow.
The soil test shows nitrogen deficiency. Should she add manure, fertiliser, or both?

steps.title: Plant nutrients (16)
steps.body:
- From **air**: carbon, oxygen. From **water**: hydrogen.
- From **soil** (13): **macronutrients** (needed in large amounts) — **nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium, sulphur**; **micronutrients** (small amounts) — **iron, manganese, boron, zinc, copper, molybdenum, chlorine**.
Deficiency affects growth, reproduction and disease resistance.

steps.title: Manure
steps.body:
Made by decomposition of animal excreta and plant waste. Provides nutrients in **small amounts** and large amounts of **organic matter (humus)**: improves soil structure, water-holding capacity of sandy soils and drainage of clayey soils; helps soil organisms; recycles farm waste.
- **Compost**: farm waste (livestock excreta, vegetable waste, straw, eradicated weeds) decomposed in pits. **Vermicompost**: compost made using **earthworms**.
- **Green manure**: green plants like **sun hemp** or **guar** are grown and ploughed back into the soil before sowing; adds nitrogen and phosphorus.

steps.title: Fertilisers
steps.body:
Commercially produced plant nutrients supplying **N, P, K**. They give quick, high yields but must be applied carefully (dose, time, pre- and post-application precautions). Excess use causes **water pollution** (washed away by irrigation) and, over time, reduces soil fertility (soil organisms and organic matter are not replenished).
**Organic farming**: minimal or no chemical fertilisers, pesticides, herbicides; maximum use of organic manures, recycled farm wastes, bio-agents (blue-green algae for bio-fertiliser, neem leaves or turmeric as bio-pesticides in grain storage), and healthy cropping systems.

steps.title: Solved: manure vs fertiliser
steps.body: Manure: organic, rich in humus, slow nutrient release, improves soil structure, cheap, nutrients not specific. Fertiliser: inorganic, nutrient-specific (N, P, K), fast acting, does not add humus, can pollute water if overused.

steps.title: Solved: identify
steps.body: Earthworms used → vermicompost. Sun hemp ploughed in → green manure. Urea → nitrogen fertiliser.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling iron a macronutrient.
- Saying fertilisers improve soil structure (they don't add organic matter).
- Forgetting C, H, O come from air and water.

activity.prompt: Macronutrient or micronutrient?

quiz.q: Number of nutrients essential for plants
quiz.why: Plants need 16 nutrients for growth. Of these, 13 come from the soil and the rest from air and water.

quiz.q: Nutrients supplied by air
quiz.why: Carbon and oxygen come from the air, and hydrogen from water. The other 13 come from the soil.

quiz.q: Vermicompost is made using
quiz.why: Vermicompost is made by earthworms feeding on and breaking down plant and animal waste. It enriches the soil.

quiz.q: Sun hemp is used as
quiz.why: Sun hemp is grown and ploughed back into the soil as green manure. It adds nutrients and organic matter.

quiz.q: Excessive fertiliser use can cause
quiz.why: Excess fertilisers run off into water bodies and pollute them. They don't improve soil structure or humus.

quiz.q: A micronutrient is
quiz.why: Manganese is a micronutrient, needed in small amounts. Nitrogen, potassium and magnesium are needed in large amounts.

scenes.text: The monsoon fails in Ramesh's district in August.
Farmers with wells and a village check-dam save their crop; others lose it. Irrigation and smart cropping reduce risk.

steps.title: Irrigation
steps.body:
Most Indian agriculture depends on timely monsoon rain. Irrigation systems:
- **Wells**: dug wells (shallow water-bearing strata) and tube wells (deeper strata), with pumps.
- **Canals**: water from reservoirs or rivers via main canal, branch canals and distributaries.
- **River lift systems**: water drawn directly from rivers where canal flow is insufficient.
- **Tanks**: small storage reservoirs for run-off.
Also **rainwater harvesting** and **watershed management** — small check-dams that increase groundwater and reduce run-off.

steps.title: Cropping patterns
steps.body:
- **Mixed cropping**: two or more crops grown **simultaneously on the same field** (wheat + gram, wheat + mustard, groundnut + sunflower) — reduces risk of total crop failure.
- **Inter-cropping**: two or more crops on the same field **in a definite row pattern** (e.g. one row of crop A, two rows of crop B), with different nutrient needs, e.g. soybean + maize, pearl millet (bajra) + cowpea (lobia). Pesticide application and harvesting are easier, and nutrients are used well.
- **Crop rotation**: growing different crops on a piece of land in a **pre-planned succession** (e.g. a legume after a cereal restores nitrogen). Two or three crops can be grown per year depending on duration and water.

steps.title: Solved: which pattern?
steps.body: Rows of maize alternating with rows of soybean → inter-cropping. Wheat and mustard seeds mixed and sown together → mixed cropping. Rice in kharif, then gram in rabi on the same field → crop rotation.

steps.title: Solved: why grow a legume in rotation?
steps.body: Legumes (gram, pea, pulses) host nitrogen-fixing bacteria in their root nodules, which replenish soil nitrogen used by cereals.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing mixed cropping (no row pattern) with inter-cropping (definite rows).
- Saying crop rotation means rotating plants physically.

activity.prompt: Match the term with its description
pairs: Two crops sown together, no fixed rows
Two crops in a definite row pattern

quiz.q: Wheat + gram sown together on the same field
quiz.why: Growing two or more crops such as wheat and gram together on the same field is mixed cropping. In inter-cropping, they are in definite row patterns.

quiz.q: Soybean + maize in alternate rows
quiz.why: Soybean and maize grown in alternate rows is inter-cropping, as the pattern is fixed. Mixed cropping has no set pattern.

quiz.q: Benefit of mixed cropping
options: reduces risk of total crop failure
quiz.why: With mixed cropping, if one crop fails, the other may survive. This reduces the risk of total crop failure.

quiz.q: Small check-dams are part of
quiz.why: Small check-dams hold back water and let it soak into the ground, which is part of watershed management. They increase groundwater.

quiz.q: A legume in crop rotation helps by
quiz.why: Legumes have bacteria in their roots that fix nitrogen, so growing them in rotation adds nitrogen to the soil.

lessons.title: Crop protection and storage of grains

scenes.text: A cooperative stores 50 tonnes of wheat; months later, some sacks are damp, mouldy and chewed by rats.
Cleaning, drying, fumigation and good stores could have saved the grain.

steps.title: Weeds, pests and diseases
steps.body:
- **Weeds**: unwanted plants that compete for food, space and light, e.g. *Xanthium* (gokhroo), *Parthenium* (gajar ghas), *Cyperus rotundus* (motha). Removed mechanically, by preventive methods (proper seed-bed, timely sowing, inter-cropping, crop rotation) or with weedicides.
- **Insect pests** attack by (i) cutting roots, stems and leaves, (ii) sucking cell sap, (iii) boring into stems and fruits.
- **Diseases** are caused by bacteria, fungi and viruses — spread through soil, water and air.
Control: **pesticides** (herbicides, insecticides, fungicides) used carefully; preventive methods like resistant varieties and summer ploughing (deep ploughing to destroy weeds and pests).

steps.title: Storage of grains
steps.body:
Losses are caused by **biotic** factors (insects, rodents, fungi, mites, bacteria) and **abiotic** factors (inappropriate moisture and temperature). They cause degradation in quality, loss in weight, poor germination, discolouration and poor marketability.
Preventive and control measures: strict **cleaning** of produce, proper **drying** (first in sunlight, then in shade), and **fumigation** with chemicals that kill pests. Warehouses (godowns) are kept clean and dry.

steps.title: Solved: identify the problem
steps.body: Holes in brinjal fruit → borer pests. Grain sacks warm and damp with fungus → abiotic factors (moisture, temperature) leading to fungal attack. Parthenium spreading in a field → weed competition.

steps.title: Solved: a storage plan
steps.body: 1) Clean and dry the grain to low moisture. 2) Store in clean, dry, rodent-proof godowns on raised platforms. 3) Fumigate if pests appear. 4) Inspect regularly.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Over-using pesticides (harms health and environment).
- Storing grain while still damp.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to store harvested grain safely
items: Clean the produce
Dry it in sunlight, then shade
Store in a clean, dry, rodent-proof godown
Fumigate if pests appear
Inspect regularly

quiz.q: Parthenium (gajar ghas) is a
quiz.why: Parthenium (gajar ghas) is a weed, an unwanted plant in the field that competes with crops.

quiz.q: Insects damage crops by all EXCEPT
quiz.why: Insects damage crops by sucking sap, boring into stems and cutting leaves, but fixing nitrogen is done by certain bacteria, not insects.

quiz.q: Abiotic causes of storage loss
quiz.why: Moisture and temperature are abiotic factors that can spoil stored grain. Insects, rats, fungi and mites are biotic.

quiz.q: Killing storage pests with chemical fumes is
quiz.why: Killing pests with chemical fumes in a closed space is fumigation. It is used for storing grain.

quiz.q: Deep ploughing in summer helps to
quiz.why: Deep ploughing in summer exposes weeds and pests to sun and kills them. It prepares the field.

lessons.title: Animal husbandry: cattle, poultry, fish and bees (extension)

story.title: The farm that does it all

scenes.text: Shanti's family farm earns from milk, eggs, a fish pond and bee boxes beside the mustard field.
Each needs different care — shelter, feed, disease control and good breeds.

steps.title: Cattle farming
steps.body: Two species: cows (*Bos indicus*) and buffaloes (*Bubalus bubalis*). **Milch animals** give milk; **draught animals** do farm labour. Exotic breeds (e.g. **Jersey, Brown Swiss**) are chosen for long lactation; local breeds (e.g. **Red Sindhi, Sahiwal**) for disease resistance — crossing them combines both. Needs: clean, well-ventilated, roofed shelter; regular cleaning and brushing; balanced feed of **roughage** (fibre) and **concentrates** (proteins, nutrients); vaccination against viral and bacterial diseases; control of external and internal parasites.

steps.title: Poultry
steps.body: Raising domestic fowl for eggs (**layers**) and meat (**broilers**). Improved varieties cross Indian breeds (e.g. **Aseel**) with exotic breeds (e.g. **Leghorn**) for number and quality of chicks, dwarfness for broiler parent stock, summer adaptation, low maintenance and smaller birds that use less feed. Broilers need protein- and vitamin-rich (A and K) feed; hygiene, proper temperature and vaccination prevent disease.

steps.title: Fish production
steps.body:
**Capture fishing** from natural resources; **culture fishery** (aquaculture) in ponds/tanks. Marine fish: pomphret, mackerel, tuna, sardines, Bombay duck; mariculture of mullets, bhetki, pearl spots, prawns, mussels, oysters (also for pearls). Inland: canals, ponds, reservoirs, rivers, estuaries.
**Composite fish culture**: 5–6 species in one pond, each using a different food zone so there is no competition — **catla** (surface), **rohu** (middle zone), **mrigal** and **common carp** (bottom), **grass carp** (weeds), with silver carp also used. A problem: some of these fish breed only during the monsoon, so pure seed supply is limited — now solved by hormonal stimulation of breeding in ponds.

steps.title: Bee-keeping (apiculture)
steps.body: Low-investment income from **honey** and **wax**. Varieties: *Apis cerana indica* (Indian bee), *A. dorsata* (rock bee), *A. florea* (little bee) and the Italian bee *A. mellifera*, preferred for high honey collection, gentleness (stings less), staying long in a hive and good breeding. **Pasturage** (flowers available) decides the quantity and the taste of honey.

steps.title: Solved: composite fish culture
steps.body: Why stock catla, rohu and mrigal together? They feed at the surface, middle and bottom respectively, so all of the pond's food is used and the fish don't compete — yield rises.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying broilers are reared for eggs (layers are).
- Saying composite culture uses one species.
- Saying honey taste is the same everywhere (depends on pasturage).

activity.prompt: Match the term

quiz.q: Draught animals are used for
quiz.why: Draught animals, like bullocks, are used for farm labour such as ploughing and carrying loads.

quiz.q: A cattle feed rich in fibre is called
quiz.why: Roughage is cattle feed rich in fibre, like fodder. Concentrates are rich in proteins and other nutrients.

quiz.q: In composite fish culture, bottom feeders include
quiz.why: In composite fish culture, mrigal and common carp are bottom feeders. Catla feeds at the surface and rohu in the middle.

quiz.q: The Italian bee is preferred because it
options: collects more honey and stings less
quiz.why: The Italian bee is preferred because it collects more honey and stings less. It also breeds well.

quiz.q: Pasturage in bee-keeping refers to
options: flowers available for nectar and pollen
quiz.why: Pasturage means the flowers available for the bees to collect nectar and pollen. Honey quality depends on it.

quiz.q: Aseel is a
quiz.why: Aseel is an Indian breed of poultry, known for its fighting qualities and meat. It is not a fish, cattle or bee.

questions.q: Rabi crops are sown in
questions.why: Rabi crops are sown in winter, around November, and harvested in spring. Kharif crops are sown in June-July.

questions.q: Which is a kharif crop?
questions.why: Paddy is a kharif crop, sown in the rainy season. Mustard, wheat and gram are rabi crops.

questions.q: Number of macronutrients obtained from soil
questions.why: Of the 13 nutrients from the soil, 6 are macronutrients (needed in large amounts) and 7 are micronutrients.

questions.q: Compost made with earthworms
questions.why: Compost made using earthworms is vermicompost. Humus is the dark organic part of the soil and urea is a fertiliser.

questions.q: Oilseeds provide mainly
questions.why: Oilseeds provide mainly fats, as in oils from groundnut and mustard. Pulses give proteins.

questions.q: Inter-cropping means crops grown
options: in a definite row pattern on the same field
questions.why: Inter-cropping means growing two or more crops in a definite pattern of rows on the same field. Mixed cropping has no pattern.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Mixed cropping reduces the risk of total crop failure. Reason (R): If one crop fails due to weather or pests, the other may survive.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. If one crop fails due to weather or pests, the other may survive, so total failure is less likely.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Excessive use of fertilisers improves soil fertility in the long run. Reason (R): Fertilisers add organic matter to the soil.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are false. Excess fertilisers do not add organic matter, and in the long run they can reduce soil fertility.

questions.q: Which pair are both micronutrients?
questions.why: Iron (Fe) and zinc (Zn) are micronutrients, needed in small amounts. K, Ca, Mg, S, N and P are macronutrients.

questions.q: A shorter maturity duration of a crop variety helps the farmer to
questions.why: A shorter maturity time lets the farmer grow more crops each year on the same field. It also saves water and labour.

questions.q: Biotic factors causing storage loss include
questions.why: Rodents and fungi are biotic factors that damage stored grain. Moisture, temperature and sunlight are abiotic.

questions.q: Case: A village's groundwater falls each year. Building small check-dams on local streams mainly helps by
options: increasing groundwater recharge and reducing run-off
questions.why: Check-dams hold back water and let it percolate, which recharges groundwater and reduces run-off. They don't add fertiliser or kill pests.

questions.q: Case: A farmer grows rice in kharif and wants to restore soil nitrogen before the next rice crop. The best rabi crop
questions.why: Gram, a legume, fixes nitrogen with the help of root bacteria, so it restores the soil nitrogen used by rice. Wheat and mustard take up nitrogen.

questions.q: Case: A fish farmer stocks only catla in a pond and finds bottom food unused. Adding which fish would best use it?
questions.why: Catla feeds at the surface, so the bottom food is unused. Mrigal and common carp are bottom feeders and would use it.

questions.q: A dairy farmer wants long lactation and disease resistance in one animal. Best approach
options: cross an exotic breed like Jersey with a local breed like Sahiwal
questions.why: Correct answer: cross an exotic breed like Jersey with a local breed like Sahiwal.

questions.q: Which statement about organic farming is correct?
options: It uses bio-agents such as blue-green algae and neem
questions.why: Organic farming uses natural methods, such as manure, crop rotation and bio-agents like blue-green algae and neem. It avoids chemical pesticides.

courses.summary: One-page fact and formula sheets for the chemistry, biology and physics chapters of Class 9 Science, exam strategy, two mock papers and a full mixed test.
outcomes: Recall the key definitions, formulas and units of every chapter
Solve numericals on motion, force, gravitation, work–energy and sound quickly
Answer assertion–reason and case-based questions confidently

scenes.text: Kiran's chemistry test is tomorrow and she keeps mixing up colloids and suspensions.
One compact sheet with every definition side by side fixes the confusion.

steps.title: Matter and purity
steps.body:
- Particles: very small, spaces between, always moving (faster when hot), attract each other. Diffusion fastest in gases.
- K = °C + 273. Ice melts at 273 K; water boils at 373 K. Latent heat: fusion (solid → liquid), vaporisation (liquid → gas). Sublimation: camphor, naphthalene, NH₄Cl, iodine; dry ice = solid CO₂.
- Evaporation ↑ with surface area, temperature, wind; ↓ with humidity; causes cooling.
- Solution (< 1 nm, no Tyndall), colloid (1–1000 nm, Tyndall, centrifuge), suspension (visible, settles, filterable).
- Mass % = solute/solution × 100. Compounds: fixed ratio, new properties; mixtures: variable, keep properties.

steps.title: Atoms and the atom
steps.body:
- Conservation of mass (Lavoisier); constant proportions (Proust; H : O = 1 : 8 in water). Dalton's atomic theory.
- 1 u = 1/12 mass of C-12. Molecular mass = sum of atomic masses (H₂O 18, CO₂ 44, H₂SO₄ 98, NaCl 58.5).
- Criss-cross valencies: Al₂O₃, Ca(OH)₂, (NH₄)₂SO₄.
- e⁻ (Thomson), canal rays/p⁺ (Goldstein), n (Chadwick 1932). Rutherford: nucleus, mostly empty space. Bohr: fixed orbits, no radiation.
- Shell capacity 2n²; outermost ≤ 8. Valency = valence e⁻ or 8 − valence e⁻.
- A = p + n; isotopes same Z (U-235 fuel, Co-60 cancer, I-131 goitre); isobars same A (⁴⁰Ca, ⁴⁰Ar).

steps.title: Quick drill
steps.body: 1) 27 °C = 300 K. 2) 20 g salt in 180 g water → 10%. 3) Formula unit mass of CaCl₂ = 111 u. 4) S (16): 2, 8, 6, valency 2. 5) Neutrons in ³⁵Cl = 18.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding instead of subtracting 273 (or vice versa).
- Dividing by solvent mass in concentration.
- Calling milk a solution.

cards.back: scattering of light by colloid/suspension particles
heat to melt 1 kg at its melting point
1/12 of the mass of a C-12 atom
same atomic number, different mass number
same mass number, different atomic numbers

quiz.q: Dry ice is
quiz.why: Dry ice is solid carbon dioxide. It sublimes straight to gas, leaving no liquid.

quiz.q: Colloid particle size
quiz.why: Colloid particles have a size between 1 and 1000 nm. They are larger than particles of a true solution, but smaller than those of a suspension.

quiz.q: Molecular mass of H₂SO₄
Valency of chlorine (2, 8, 7)
quiz.why: Chlorine (2, 8, 7) needs 1 more electron to complete its octet, so its valency is 1.

quiz.q: Isotope used for nuclear-reactor fuel
quiz.why: U-235 is a fissile isotope: its nucleus splits when it absorbs a neutron, releasing energy and more neutrons for a chain reaction. Co-60, I-131 and C-14 are used in medicine, therapy or dating, not as reactor fuel.

scenes.text: Biology answers need exact words — 'selectively permeable', 'suicide bags', 'apical meristem'.
This sheet lists the words examiners look for.

steps.title: Cell
steps.body:
- Hooke 1665 (cork); Leeuwenhoek 1674; Brown 1831 (nucleus); Purkinje 1839 (protoplasm); Schleiden & Schwann (cell theory); Virchow 1855 (cells from cells).
- Plasma membrane: selectively permeable (lipids + proteins). Diffusion; osmosis (water across a membrane); hypotonic → swells, isotonic → no change, hypertonic → shrinks. Plasmolysis in plant cells.
- Cell wall: cellulose. Prokaryote: nucleoid, no membrane-bound organelles.
- ER (RER proteins, SER lipids/detox), Golgi (package/dispatch), lysosome (suicide bag), mitochondria (ATP, own DNA), plastids (chloroplast/leucoplast, own DNA), vacuole.
- Mitosis: 2 identical cells; meiosis: 4 cells, half chromosomes (gametes).

steps.title: Tissues
steps.body:
- Meristem: apical (length), lateral/cambium (girth), intercalary (base of leaves/internodes); no vacuoles.
- Parenchyma (store; chlorenchyma, aerenchyma), collenchyma (flexibility), sclerenchyma (dead, lignin). Epidermis (cutin, stomata), cork (suberin).
- Xylem: tracheids, vessels, parenchyma, fibres — water up. Phloem: sieve tubes, companion cells, parenchyma, fibres (only dead part) — food both ways.
- Epithelium: squamous, stratified (skin), columnar (intestine; ciliated in airways), cuboidal (kidney tubules), glandular. Connective: blood, bone, ligament (bone–bone), tendon (muscle–bone), cartilage, areolar, adipose. Muscles: striated (voluntary, multinucleate), smooth (involuntary, spindle), cardiac (branched). Neuron: dendrites, cell body, axon.

steps.title: Food resources
steps.body:
- Kharif (June–Oct): paddy, soybean, maize, cotton, pulses (arhar, moong, urad). Rabi (Nov–Apr): wheat, gram, peas, mustard, linseed.
- 16 nutrients: C, H, O from air/water; macro N, P, K, Ca, Mg, S; micro Fe, Mn, B, Zn, Cu, Mo, Cl.
- Manure (compost, vermicompost, green manure) vs fertiliser (NPK). Mixed cropping, inter-cropping, crop rotation. Storage: clean, dry, fumigate.

steps.title: Quick drill
steps.body: 1) Organelle with digestive enzymes → lysosome. 2) RBC in pure water → swells/bursts. 3) Coconut husk → sclerenchyma. 4) Ligament joins → bone to bone. 5) Wheat → rabi.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ligament vs tendon.
- Cutin (epidermis) vs suberin (cork).
- Kharif vs rabi months.

activity.prompt: Match

quiz.q: Cell theory was proposed by
quiz.why: Schleiden (botanist) and Schwann (zoologist) proposed that all living things are made of cells. Virchow later added that new cells arise from existing cells; Hooke only observed and named cells.

quiz.q: A cell in hypertonic solution
quiz.why: In a hypertonic solution the outside has more solute, so water leaves the cell by osmosis through the membrane. Losing water makes the cell shrink; swelling or bursting happens in a hypotonic solution.

quiz.q: The only dead component of phloem
quiz.why: Sieve tubes, companion cells and phloem parenchyma are living cells. Phloem fibres are sclerenchyma with thick lignified walls and no living contents, so they are the dead component.

quiz.q: Voluntary muscles are
quiz.why: Voluntary muscles, such as those of the arms and legs, show light and dark bands under a microscope, so they are called striated. Smooth muscles are involuntary; cardiac muscle is involuntary too.

quiz.q: A micronutrient
quiz.why: Micronutrients are needed by plants in very small amounts; zinc is one. Potassium, sulphur and calcium are needed in large amounts, so they are macronutrients.

scenes.text: Arjun knows the theory but freezes on numericals.
He writes the formula, lists given values with units, substitutes and checks units — every time.

steps.title: Motion and force
steps.body:
- Speed = distance/time; 1 km/h = 5/18 m/s; average velocity (uniform a) = (u + v)/2.
- a = (v − u)/t. Graphs: slope of s–t = speed; slope of v–t = a; area under v–t = displacement.
- v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² − u² = 2as. Circular: v = 2πr/t.
- p = mv; F = ma = Δp/t; impulse F·t = Δp; action = −reaction; m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂.

steps.title: Gravitation, work and energy
steps.body:
- F = Gm₁m₂/d², G = 6.673 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²; g = GM/R² ≈ 9.8 m/s²; W = mg; Moon ≈ 1/6.
- P = F/A (Pa); upthrust = weight of fluid displaced; RD = density/1000 kg m⁻³.
- W = Fs (J); KE = ½mv²; PE = mgh; PE + KE constant in free fall; P = W/t (W); 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.

steps.title: Sound
steps.body:
- v = λν; T = 1/ν; audible 20 Hz–20 kHz; pitch ↔ frequency, loudness ↔ amplitude.
- Echo: d = vt/2, minimum distance ≈ 17.2 m (v = 344 m/s, 0.1 s). SONAR depth = vt/2. Speed: solids > liquids > gases.

steps.title: Quick drill
steps.body: 1) 90 km/h = 25 m/s. 2) From rest, a = 3 m/s² for 4 s ⇒ v = 12 m/s, s = 24 m. 3) 2 kg, F = 10 N ⇒ a = 5 m/s². 4) KE of 4 kg at 3 m/s = 18 J. 5) Echo 1.5 s, v = 340 ⇒ 255 m.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Not converting km/h, g, cm², minutes.
- Forgetting ½ in KE and s = ut + ½at², or the halving in echo/SONAR.
- Writing m/s for acceleration.

quiz.q: Area under a velocity–time graph gives
quiz.why: Velocity = displacement/time, so the area under a velocity–time graph (velocity × time) equals displacement. The slope of that graph gives acceleration, not the area.

quiz.q: A 3 kg mass accelerates at 4 m/s². Force
quiz.why: Force = mass × acceleration = 3 kg × 4 m/s² = 12 N. The other values come from dividing or adding the numbers instead of multiplying.

quiz.q: Weight of 50 kg on Earth (g = 9.8)
quiz.why: Weight = mass × g = 50 × 9.8 = 490 N. Weight is a force measured in newtons; 50 kg is the mass, which stays the same everywhere.

quiz.q: PE of 5 kg at 4 m (g = 10)
quiz.why: Potential energy = mgh = 5 × 10 × 4 = 200 J. Multiply mass, g and height; 40 J or 20 J come from leaving out a factor.

quiz.q: λ for 680 Hz in air at 340 m/s
quiz.why: Wavelength = speed ÷ frequency = 340 ÷ 680 = 0.5 m. A higher frequency at the same speed gives a shorter wavelength.

scenes.text: Set a 25-minute timer. No notes.
Mark yourself, then revise the chapter for every miss.

steps.title: How to use
steps.body: 8 mixed questions across chemistry, biology and physics. Write formula → values → substitution → answer with unit for numericals.

steps.title: Strategy
steps.body:
- Attempt sure questions first.
- For assertion–reason: judge A, then R, then whether R explains A.
- For case-based questions: underline the data in the case before reading the options.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Missing units.
- Reading 'NOT' or 'EXCEPT' too quickly.

activity.prompt: Before you start
items: Timer on 25 minutes
Rough sheet ready
Formula sheets closed
Plan: easy first, check units at the end

quiz.q: Which evaporates fastest?
options: water spread on a plate on a windy sunny day
quiz.why: Evaporation is fastest with a large surface area, high temperature, wind and low humidity. Water spread on a plate on a windy, sunny day has all of these; the other cases limit surface, air movement or dryness.

quiz.q: A solution has 15 g solute in 135 g water. Mass %
quiz.why: Mass % = solute ÷ solution × 100. The solution is 15 + 135 = 150 g, so 15/150 × 100 = 10%. The common slip, 15/135, ignores the solute's own mass.

quiz.q: Formula of aluminium sulphate
quiz.why: Aluminium is Al³⁺ and sulphate is SO₄²⁻. Criss-cross the charges: 2 Al³⁺ (+6) balance 3 SO₄²⁻ (−6), giving Al₂(SO₄)₃.

quiz.q: Electrons in O²⁻ (Z = 8)
quiz.why: Oxygen has Z = 8, so 8 electrons in the atom. O²⁻ has gained 2 electrons, so 8 + 2 = 10 electrons, the same as neon.

quiz.q: Organelle that packages and dispatches
quiz.why: The Golgi apparatus receives substances made in the cell, packs them into vesicles and sends them to where they are needed. Lysosomes digest waste, ribosomes make proteins and the nucleus holds DNA.

quiz.q: A car from 0 to 30 m/s in 10 s: distance
quiz.why: Starting from rest, s = ½ × v × t = ½ × 30 × 10 = 150 m using the average speed 15 m/s. Using 30 × 10 = 300 m wrongly assumes the car moved at top speed throughout.

quiz.q: A gun of 5 kg fires a 20 g bullet at 500 m/s. Recoil speed
quiz.why: Momentum is conserved. Bullet momentum = 0.02 × 500 = 10 kg m/s, so the gun recoils with 10 ÷ 5 = 2 m/s in the opposite direction.

quiz.q: SONAR echo after 2.4 s, v = 1500 m/s. Depth
quiz.why: The sound travels to the sea bed and back, so depth = v × t ÷ 2 = 1500 × 2.4 ÷ 2 = 1800 m. 3600 m forgets to halve for the round trip.

scenes.text: A week later, try the second paper.
Compare your score with Mock Paper 1 and update your error log.

steps.title: How to use
steps.body: Another 8 mixed questions, slightly harder. 25 minutes.

steps.title: Error log
steps.body: For each mistake write: chapter, what went wrong (concept / calculation / reading), and the fix. Review the log before the final test.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Revising only favourite chapters.
- Not re-attempting wrong questions.

activity.prompt: After the paper
items: Marked all answers
Updated error log
Revisited weak chapters
Ready for the final mixed test

quiz.q: Steam at 100 °C burns more than water at 100 °C because
options: it carries extra latent heat of vaporisation
quiz.why: Steam at 100 °C holds extra latent heat of vaporisation (about 2260 J per gram) that it releases when it condenses on skin. Water at the same temperature lacks this extra heat, so steam burns more.

quiz.q: A mixture of ethanol (351 K) and water (373 K) is separated by
quiz.why: The boiling points differ by 22 K, which is small, so simple distillation cannot separate them cleanly. Fractional distillation with a fractionating column is used for miscible liquids with close boiling points.

quiz.q: Average atomic mass of an element with ¹⁰X 20% and ¹¹X 80%
quiz.why: Average mass = (10 × 20 + 11 × 80)/100 = (200 + 880)/100 = 10.8 u. The result is closer to 11 because the heavier isotope is more abundant.

quiz.q: Cells of a tissue are long, dead and lignified. The tissue is
quiz.why: Sclerenchyma cells are long, dead and have lignified thick walls, giving strength. Parenchyma and collenchyma are living tissues, and meristem is made of dividing cells.

quiz.q: If the distance between two masses is halved, the gravitational force
quiz.why: Gravitational force is proportional to 1/d². Halving d gives 1/(½)² = 4, so the force becomes 4 times larger. It does not simply double.

quiz.q: A 60 kg man climbs 10 m in 20 s (g = 10). Power
quiz.why: Work = mgh = 60 × 10 × 10 = 6000 J. Power = work ÷ time = 6000 ÷ 20 = 300 W. 6000 W forgets to divide by time.

quiz.q: Velocity 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 4 s; distance covered
quiz.why: Average velocity = (10 + 30)/2 = 20 m/s, so distance = 20 × 4 = 80 m. Using only the final speed would overestimate the distance.

quiz.q: Composite fish culture works because the species
options: feed in different zones of the pond
quiz.why: In composite fish culture, species such as catla, rohu and mrigal feed at different levels of the pond (surface, middle, bottom). They do not compete much, so the pond gives more fish.

questions.q: Which is a chemical change?
questions.why: Burning wood forms new substances such as ash, carbon dioxide and water vapour, and it cannot be reversed. Melting, evaporating and dissolving only change the state or mixing, so they are physical changes.

questions.q: Symbol of sodium
questions.why: The symbol of sodium comes from its Latin name natrium, so it is Na. S stands for sulphur and N for nitrogen.

questions.q: Plant cell wall is made of
questions.why: The plant cell wall is made of cellulose, a tough carbohydrate. Chitin forms fungal walls and insect shells; lipids and proteins are not the main wall material.

questions.q: SI unit of power
questions.why: Power is the rate of doing work, and its SI unit is the watt (1 J/s). Newton is for force, pascal for pressure and joule for energy.

questions.q: Convert 300 K to °C
questions.why: °C = K − 273, so 300 − 273 = 27 °C. Adding 273 would give 573, which is wrong for this direction.

questions.q: Valency of aluminium
questions.why: Aluminium has 3 valence electrons (2, 8, 3), and it loses them to form Al³⁺, so its valency is 3.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Mitochondria can make some of their own proteins. Reason (R): They have their own DNA and ribosomes.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both statements are true: mitochondria hold their own DNA and ribosomes, so they can make some of their own proteins. The reason directly explains the assertion.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Sound travels faster in steel than in air. Reason (R): Sound needs a medium to travel.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both statements are true. Sound is faster in steel because steel is much stiffer and its particles transmit vibrations faster. Needing a medium is true, but it does not explain why steel is faster than air.

questions.q: Molecular mass of C₂H₅OH
questions.why: C₂H₅OH: 2 × 12 + 5 × 1 + 16 + 1 = 24 + 5 + 16 + 1 = 46 u. Add the mass of every atom in the formula, including the hydrogen in OH.

questions.q: Tissue connecting muscle to bone
questions.why: A tendon joins muscle to bone. A ligament joins bone to bone, and cartilage is a smooth cushioning tissue at joints.

questions.q: A body of mass 2 kg moves at 10 m/s. Its momentum and KE
questions.why: Momentum = mv = 2 × 10 = 20 kg m/s. KE = ½mv² = ½ × 2 × 100 = 100 J. Other options mix up the formulas or forget the square.

questions.q: Case: In Rutherford's experiment, if 1 in 12 000 α-particles bounced back, this mainly shows
options: the nucleus is tiny, dense and positive
questions.why: Most α-particles passed straight through, but very few bounced back. This showed that the positive charge and mass are packed into a tiny, dense nucleus. It did not show that atoms are solid.

questions.q: Case: A 10 kg block on a 0.5 m² base is stacked with an identical block (g = 10). Pressure on the floor
questions.why: The floor carries both blocks: weight = 20 kg × 10 = 200 N. Pressure = force ÷ area = 200 ÷ 0.5 = 400 Pa. Using only one block would give 200 Pa.

questions.q: A ball is thrown up at 25 m/s (g = 10). Time to reach maximum height and the height
questions.why: At the top v = 0, so t = u/g = 25/10 = 2.5 s. Height = u²/2g = 625/20 = 31.25 m. Time up is u/g, not 2u/g (that is the full flight).

questions.q: A sea-bed is 3000 m deep; SONAR speed 1500 m/s. Echo time
questions.why: The echo covers the depth twice, so t = 2d/v = 2 × 3000 ÷ 1500 = 4 s. Using d/v = 2 s forgets the return trip.

questions.q: An element has configuration 2, 8, 8, 2. Its atomic number, valency and name
questions.why: The configuration 2, 8, 8, 2 has 2 + 8 + 8 + 2 = 20 electrons, so the atomic number is 20 (calcium). It has 2 outer electrons, so its valency is 2.

questions.q: A 1000 kg car at 72 km/h stops in 50 m. Average braking force
questions.why: 72 km/h = 20 m/s. From v² = u² + 2as, 0 = 400 + 2a(50), so a = −4 m/s². Force = ma = 1000 × 4 = 4000 N.

questions.q: A piece of iron of volume 100 cm³ (density 7.9 g/cm³) is fully immersed in water. Upthrust (g = 10)
questions.why: Upthrust equals the weight of water displaced. 100 cm³ of water has mass 100 g = 0.1 kg, so upthrust = 0.1 × 10 = 1 N. The density of iron is not needed.

questions.q: A lamp of 100 W and a heater of 1.5 kW each run 4 hours. Total energy
questions.why: Energy = power × time. Lamp: 0.1 kW × 4 h = 0.4 kWh. Heater: 1.5 kW × 4 h = 6 kWh. Total = 0.4 + 6 = 6.4 kWh; convert 100 W to 0.1 kW first.

school-c9-social-a.title: Class 9 Social Science · History (India and the Contemporary World – I)
school-c9-social-a.description: Chapter-by-chapter Class 9 History: the French Revolution, socialism and the Russian Revolution, Nazism, forest societies and pastoralists — explained fully with solved answers, common mistakes and chapter tests.

courses.title: Ch 1 · The French Revolution
courses.summary: Why France exploded in 1789, how the monarchy fell, what the Jacobins and the Terror were, and the ideas of liberty and equality the Revolution left to the world.
outcomes: Learners can describe French society under the Old Regime and its three estates
Learners can sequence the main events of 1789–1815
Learners can explain the role of philosophers and the middle class
Learners can evaluate what the Revolution changed for women, slaves and everyday life

lessons.title: French society in the late 18th century

scenes.text: In 1788 Jacques, a peasant near Paris, pays rent to the lord, a tenth of his grain to the Church, and the taille to the state.
Bread prices jump after a bad harvest. His wages have not risen. He wonders why the rich priests and nobles pay almost nothing.

steps.title: The Old Regime
steps.body:
In 1774 **Louis XVI** of the Bourbon family became king of France. He inherited an **empty treasury**: long wars and help to the thirteen American colonies in their war against Britain had doubled France's debt to more than 2 billion livres.

French society before 1789 is called the **Old Regime (ancien régime)**. It was divided into three **estates**:
- **First Estate** – clergy (Church)
- **Second Estate** – nobility
- **Third Estate** – everyone else: big businessmen, merchants, lawyers, court officials, peasants, artisans, landless labourers and servants

The first two estates were born into **privileges**, the most important being **exemption from taxes** paid to the state.

steps.title: Who paid what
steps.body:
- **Tithes**: a tax the Church collected from peasants — one-tenth of agricultural produce.
- **Taille**: a direct tax paid to the state, only by the Third Estate.
- **Indirect taxes** on everyday goods like salt and tobacco.
- Feudal dues to nobles, and unpaid labour (in the lord's house, fields, army or road building).

The peasants made up about 90% of the population, yet only a small number owned the land they cultivated; about 60% of land was owned by nobles, the Church and richer Third Estate members.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. What was a 'subsistence crisis'? Why did it happen in France? (3 marks)**
- Step 1 – Define: a situation where the basic means of livelihood are endangered.
- Step 2 – Cause: population rose from about 23 million in 1715 to 28 million in 1789, so demand for grain rose faster than production.
- Step 3 – Effect: bread prices rose quickly, wages did not keep pace, and drought or hail made things worse. The gap between rich and poor widened.

**Q2. Why was the Third Estate angry? (3 marks)**
- It alone paid taxes to the state (taille) and tithes to the Church.
- It had no privileges, though it did most of the work.
- Its richer members (the new middle class) were educated and wanted position by merit, not birth.

steps.title: A growing middle class and new ideas
steps.body:
Merchants, manufacturers, lawyers and administrators grew rich through trade and expanding industries (like woollen and silk textiles). They believed no group should be privileged by birth.

Philosophers shaped their thinking:
- **John Locke** (*Two Treatises of Government*) rejected the **divine and absolute right** of the monarch.
- **Jean-Jacques Rousseau** (*The Social Contract*) proposed government based on a contract between people and their representatives.
- **Montesquieu** (*The Spirit of the Laws*) proposed dividing power among the **legislature, executive and judiciary**.

These ideas spread in salons, coffee-houses, books and newspapers, often read aloud to people who could not read.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the First Estate was the nobility — it was the **clergy**. Nobility = Second Estate.
- Writing that the Third Estate was only peasants — it also included rich merchants and lawyers.
- Mixing up the books: *Social Contract* = Rousseau; *Spirit of the Laws* = Montesquieu; *Two Treatises* = Locke.
- Forgetting that tithes went to the **Church**, taille to the **state**.

activity.prompt: Match each thinker with the idea or book
pairs: Division of power into three organs

quiz.q: Who belonged to the First Estate?
quiz.why: In the old French society the clergy formed the First Estate, nobles the Second, and the rest (peasants, merchants, workers) the Third. So the Church people were the First Estate.

quiz.q: Which tax was paid directly to the state by the Third Estate?
quiz.why: The taille was a direct tax paid to the state, and it fell on the Third Estate. The tithe went to the Church, and corvée was forced labour; the livre was a currency.

quiz.q: Who wrote 'The Spirit of the Laws'?
quiz.why: Montesquieu wrote 'The Spirit of the Laws' and proposed dividing power among the legislature, executive and judiciary. Rousseau wrote 'The Social Contract' and Locke 'Two Treatises of Government'.

quiz.q: A main reason for France's empty treasury under Louis XVI was:
options: Long wars including aid to American colonies
quiz.why: War expenses, including helping the American colonies, pushed debt above 2 billion livres.

quiz.q: A subsistence crisis means:
options: The basic means of livelihood are endangered
quiz.why: A subsistence crisis means ordinary people's basic means of survival, such as food, are in danger. In France, a rising population, poor harvests and costly bread caused this.

story.title: A locked hall, a tennis court

scenes.text: 20 June 1789. Delegates of the Third Estate find their meeting hall at Versailles locked.
They gather in an indoor tennis court and swear not to separate until France has a constitution.

steps.title: The Estates General
steps.body:
To raise new taxes, Louis XVI called the **Estates General** — a political body of the three estates — on **5 May 1789**. It had last met in **1614**.

Each estate traditionally had **one vote**. The Third Estate (about 600 members) demanded voting **by each member**, so each member would have one vote. When the king refused, its members walked out.

On **20 June 1789** they assembled in an indoor tennis court at Versailles, declared themselves the **National Assembly**, and took the **Tennis Court Oath**. Leaders: **Mirabeau** (a noble) and **Abbé Sieyès** (a priest, who wrote the pamphlet *What is the Third Estate?*).

steps.title: 14 July 1789 and the Great Fear
steps.body:
Rumours spread that the king would order troops to fire on citizens. On **14 July 1789** an agitated crowd stormed and destroyed the **Bastille**, a fortress-prison hated as a symbol of the king's despotic power.

In the countryside, rumours that lords' bands were coming to destroy crops led to the **Great Fear**: peasants attacked chateaux, looted grain and burnt records of manorial dues. Many nobles fled.

On **4 August 1789** the Assembly abolished the feudal system of obligations and taxes, abolished tithes and confiscated Church lands.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Why was the Bastille stormed? (2 marks)**
It stood for the king's despotic power; people feared troops would be ordered to fire on them, so they attacked it on 14 July 1789.

**Q2. Describe the Tennis Court Oath. (3 marks)**
- Step 1 – Background: the king refused vote-per-member at the Estates General.
- Step 2 – Event: on 20 June 1789 Third Estate representatives met in an indoor tennis court at Versailles.
- Step 3 – Significance: they declared themselves the National Assembly and swore not to disperse till they drafted a constitution limiting the monarch's powers.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The Estates General was **not** an elected parliament with law-making power; it only met when the king called it.
- The Bastille was stormed on **14 July** (French National Day), not 4 August.
- Sieyès wrote *What is the Third Estate?* — not *The Social Contract*.

steps.title: Memory hook
steps.body: **5 May → 20 June → 14 July → 4 August** (1789): meet, swear, storm, abolish.

activity.prompt: Put the events of 1789 in order

events.text: Tennis Court Oath; National Assembly declared

quiz.q: When had the Estates General last met before 1789?
quiz.why: The Estates General had not met since 1614, so it was a rarely used body. Louis XVI called it in 1789 to approve new taxes.

quiz.q: What did the Third Estate demand at the Estates General?
quiz.why: The Third Estate wanted each member to have one vote, since it had far more members than the other two estates combined. The old system gave one vote per estate, which let the two privileged estates win.

quiz.q: Who wrote 'What is the Third Estate?'
quiz.why: Abbé Sieyès, a priest, wrote the pamphlet 'What is the Third Estate?', which argued that the common people were the real nation. Rousseau, Voltaire and Montesquieu wrote other works.

quiz.q: The Great Fear refers to:
options: Peasant panic and attacks on chateaux in 1789
quiz.why: The Great Fear was the rural panic of 1789, when rumours of brigands made peasants attack chateaux, loot grain and burn documents recording feudal dues. It was not the Terror, which came later.

quiz.q: On 4 August 1789 the Assembly:
quiz.why: On the night of 4 August 1789, the National Assembly abolished feudal obligations and tithes, and Church land was later taken over. Executing the king and crowning Napoleon happened later.

lessons.title: From constitutional monarchy to republic and Terror

scenes.text: Pierre, a 30-year-old shopkeeper who pays taxes, is told he is an 'active citizen' and may vote in 1791.
His wife Marie, who also works in the shop, is told she is a 'passive citizen'. She joins a women's club to protest.

steps.title: The Constitution of 1791
steps.body:
The National Assembly completed a constitution in **1791**. It made France a **constitutional monarchy**: the king's powers were divided among the legislature, executive and judiciary.
- Laws were made by the **National Assembly**, which was **indirectly elected**.
- Only **active citizens** could vote: men above 25 who paid taxes equal to at least 3 days of a labourer's wage. The rest — men without such property, and all women — were **passive citizens**.
- It began with the **Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen** (1789): life, freedom of speech and opinion, equality before law as natural and inalienable rights.

steps.title: War, Jacobins and the Republic
steps.body:
- **April 1792**: the Assembly declared war against **Prussia and Austria**. Volunteers marched singing the *Marseillaise*, composed by Roget de L'Isle.
- The **Jacobin club** (led by **Maximilian Robespierre**) drew in small shopkeepers, artisans and workers. Many wore long striped trousers and were called **sans-culottes** ('without knee breeches').
- **August 1792**: Jacobins stormed the Tuileries palace and held the king hostage.
- Elections were then held in which **all men over 21**, regardless of wealth, could vote. The new assembly, the **Convention**, abolished the monarchy on **21 September 1792** and declared France a **republic**.
- Louis XVI was executed for treason in **January 1793**; Queen Marie Antoinette shortly after.

steps.title: The Reign of Terror and the Directory
steps.body:
**1793–1794** is called the **Reign of Terror**. Robespierre followed a policy of severe control: people he saw as enemies of the republic were arrested and tried by a revolutionary tribunal; many were executed by guillotine. He set price ceilings on wages and prices, rationed meat and bread, forced peasants to sell grain at fixed prices, banned expensive white flour (everyone ate the 'equality bread'), and replaced Monsieur/Madame with **Citoyen/Citoyenne**.

Robespierre was convicted and executed in **July 1794**. A new constitution then created two elected councils which appointed a five-member executive called the **Directory**. Political instability under the Directory paved the way for the rise of **Napoleon Bonaparte**.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Distinguish active and passive citizens. (2 marks)**
Active citizens: men above 25 paying taxes equal to at least 3 days' wages — they could vote. Passive citizens: all others including all women — no vote.

**Q2. Why is 1793–94 called the Reign of Terror? (3 marks)**
- Robespierre's government used severe control and punishment.
- Nobles, clergy, members of other parties and even his own party who disagreed were arrested and many guillotined.
- Laws on prices, rations and dress were enforced strictly; the period ended with his own execution in July 1794.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The 1791 Constitution did **not** abolish monarchy — the Convention did, in September 1792.
- 'Sans-culottes' means *without knee breeches* (the fashion of nobles), not 'without clothes'.
- Universal adult *male* suffrage came in 1792 elections — women still could not vote.

activity.prompt: Under the 1791 Constitution, sort these people

items.text: A landless servant aged 50 who paid no taxes

quiz.q: The 1791 Constitution made France a:
quiz.why: The 1791 Constitution kept the king but limited his powers by dividing them among the legislature, executive and judiciary. A king with limited power under a constitution is a constitutional monarchy.

quiz.q: Who led the Jacobin club?
quiz.why: Maximilian Robespierre led the Jacobin club, the most famous political club of the Revolution. Mirabeau was a moderate leader, and Louis XVI was the king.

quiz.q: France was declared a republic on:
quiz.why: The Convention abolished the monarchy and declared France a republic on 21 September 1792. The king was executed in January 1793, and the Bastille fell on 14 July 1789.

quiz.q: The Directory was:
quiz.why: After Robespierre's fall, two councils appointed a five-member executive called the Directory.

quiz.q: The patriotic song 'Marseillaise' was composed by:
quiz.why: Roget de L'Isle composed the song in 1792. Volunteers from Marseilles sang it as they marched to Paris, so it became known as the Marseillaise and later France's national anthem.

lessons.title: Women, slavery, everyday life and the legacy

scenes.text: Olympe de Gouges reads the Declaration of the Rights of Man and notices it says nothing about women.
She writes her own Declaration of the Rights of Woman and Citizen and sends it to the queen and the Assembly.

steps.title: Did women gain?
steps.body:
Most Third Estate women worked as seamstresses, laundresses, sellers or domestic servants, with little education. They formed political clubs; about 60 women's clubs came up in French cities, the best known being the **Society of Revolutionary and Republican Women**.

Gains: state schools and compulsory schooling for all girls, no forced marriage, marriage as a contract, **divorce made legal**, and women could train for jobs and run small businesses.

Under the Terror women's clubs were closed and many prominent women, including **Olympe de Gouges**, were executed. French women finally won the **right to vote in 1946**.

steps.title: Abolition of slavery
steps.body:
French colonies in the Caribbean (Martinique, Guadeloupe, San Domingo) depended on enslaved Africans for tobacco, indigo, sugar and coffee. Port cities like Bordeaux and Nantes grew rich on the slave trade.
- **1794**: the Convention freed all slaves in French overseas possessions.
- About ten years later **Napoleon reintroduced slavery**.
- Slavery was **finally abolished in French colonies in 1848**.

steps.title: Everyday life and the legacy
steps.body:
After 1789, **censorship was abolished**; newspapers, pamphlets, books and printed pictures flooded towns; plays, songs and festive processions spread ideas of liberty and justice.

**Napoleon** crowned himself Emperor in **1804** and conquered much of Europe, introducing laws such as protection of private property and a uniform system of weights and measures (the decimal system). He was finally defeated at **Waterloo in 1815**.

**Legacy**: liberty and democratic rights spread across Europe in the 19th century; feudal systems were abolished; colonised peoples (for example **Tipu Sultan** and **Rammohan Roy** in India) drew on these ideas.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Which laws improved women's lives after the Revolution? (3 marks)**
Compulsory schooling for girls; marriage as a free contract and no forced marriage; legal divorce; right to train for jobs and run small businesses.

**Q2. Trace the history of slavery in French colonies. (3 marks)**
1794 – abolished by the Convention → about 10 years later reintroduced by Napoleon → 1848 – finally abolished.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Women did **not** get the vote in the Revolution — only in **1946**.
- Slavery was not abolished once and for all in 1794; remember the 1848 date.
- Napoleon was a product of the Revolution's instability but was **not** a Jacobin leader of the Terror.

statements.s: French women won the right to vote in 1946.
statements.why: This was a long struggle that continued after the Revolution.

statements.s: Napoleon permanently ended slavery.
statements.why: He reintroduced it; final abolition came in 1848.

statements.s: Censorship was abolished after 1789.
statements.why: The Declaration made freedom of speech a natural right.

statements.s: Divorce was made legal for French women during the Revolution.
statements.why: It was one of the laws that improved women's lives.

quiz.q: Who wrote a Declaration of the Rights of Woman and Citizen?
quiz.why: Olympe de Gouges wrote the Declaration of the Rights of Woman and Citizen because the 1789 Declaration of Rights of Man left women out. She demanded equal rights for women.

quiz.q: When was slavery finally abolished in French colonies?
quiz.why: Slavery was abolished in 1794 by the Convention, but Napoleon brought it back. It was finally abolished in French colonies in 1848.

quiz.q: Napoleon was finally defeated at:
quiz.why: Napoleon was finally defeated at the Battle of Waterloo in 1815. The Bastille and Versailles are not battles he lost, and Austerlitz was one of his victories.

quiz.q: Which Indian figure was influenced by revolutionary ideas from France?
quiz.why: Tipu Sultan was inspired by revolutionary France: he planted a tree of liberty and became a member of a Jacobin club. Akbar, Ashoka and Shivaji lived long before this.

quiz.q: Port towns that grew rich on the slave trade were:
quiz.why: Bordeaux and Nantes were French ports whose merchants grew rich on the slave trade, as ships carried enslaved Africans to the Caribbean colonies. Paris and Lyon are not port towns.

questions.q: The Second Estate consisted of:
questions.why: The nobility formed the Second Estate in France's old society. The clergy were the First Estate, while peasants and merchants belonged to the Third Estate.

questions.q: The Bastille was stormed on:
questions.why: The Bastille, a prison fortress seen as a symbol of royal despotism, was stormed by the Parisian crowd on 14 July 1789. This date is now France's national day.

questions.q: Louis XVI became king in:
questions.why: Louis XVI became king in 1774 at the age of 20. The Revolution broke out in 1789, and he was executed in 1793, so those years are not the start of his rule.

questions.q: Which book argued for dividing power among legislature, executive and judiciary?
questions.why: Montesquieu's 'The Spirit of the Laws' argued that power should be divided among the legislature, executive and judiciary. 'The Social Contract' is Rousseau's work on popular sovereignty.

questions.q: Who could vote under the 1791 Constitution?
options: Men over 25 paying taxes worth at least 3 days' wages
questions.why: Under the 1791 Constitution only 'active citizens', men above 25 who paid taxes equal to at least 3 days of a labourer's wages, could vote. Women and poorer men were 'passive citizens'.

questions.q: Sans-culottes were:
options: Jacobin supporters, often poorer, who wore long striped trousers
questions.why: Sans-culottes, meaning 'without knee breeches', were poorer people who wore long striped trousers, unlike nobles who wore knee breeches. They supported the Jacobins.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The Third Estate walked out of the Estates General. Reason (R): The king rejected voting by each member.
options: Both A and R true; R explains A
Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both statements are true. The Third Estate walked out because the king refused its demand for one vote per member, so the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Which happened FIRST?
options: War declared on Prussia and Austria
questions.why: April 1792 war → Sept 1792 republic → Jan 1793 execution → July 1794 Robespierre.

questions.q: Case: In 1793 a baker is forced to bake only one kind of bread from mixed grain and to sell at a fixed price. This reflects:
questions.why: Forcing bakers to bake one 'equality bread' and fixing prices was part of Robespierre's Terror-era controls. The Old Regime and the Directory did not do this, and Napoleon's Code dealt with civil law.

questions.q: Which right was NOT included in the Declaration of the Rights of Man as a natural right?
questions.why: The Declaration of the Rights of Man guaranteed rights such as life, speech and equality before law, but women were not given the vote. That is why Olympe de Gouges protested.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The Revolution gave women equal political rights. Reason (R): Women's clubs were closed during the Terror.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Women did not get equal political rights (vote only in 1946); clubs were indeed closed.

questions.q: If France's population rose from 23 million to 28 million between 1715 and 1789, the percentage increase is about:
questions.why: Increase = 28 − 23 = 5 million. Percentage = 5 ÷ 23 × 100 ≈ 21.7%, about 22%. Always divide by the original value (23), not the new one.

questions.q: Why did the middle class lead the Revolution rather than the peasants alone?
options: They were educated, wealthy and believed position should depend on merit
questions.why: The middle class was educated and wealthy, and believed that position should depend on merit, not birth. This made them the leaders and thinkers of the Third Estate, though they were not the majority.

questions.q: Case: A ruler crowns himself emperor, conquers neighbours, introduces uniform weights and measures and protects private property, but reintroduces slavery. Who and when?
questions.why: Napoleon crowned himself emperor in 1804, conquered neighbouring lands, brought uniform weights, measures and the Civil Code protecting property, and reintroduced slavery. Louis XVI and Robespierre did not do these things.

questions.q: Which statement best explains why the Directory fell?
options: Political instability let a military dictator, Napoleon, rise
questions.why: The Directory was weak and unstable, with conflicts among its members and the people. This let the military leader Napoleon take power in 1799. It did not free slaves or abolish the monarchy.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Socialism in Europe and the Russian Revolution
courses.summary: Liberals, radicals and conservatives; the rise of socialism; and how Russia moved from the Tsar to the Bolsheviks, collectivisation and a global impact.
outcomes: Learners can compare liberal, radical and conservative ideas
Learners can explain socialist ideas of Owen, Blanc and Marx
