quiz.why: India's representation is based on area: the country is divided into constituencies, each electing one representative. It is not based on religion, caste lists or profession.

quiz.q: Women's reservation in local bodies is:
quiz.why: Local bodies have at least one-third of seats reserved for women, and some states have raised it to 50%. 'Half everywhere' is not required by law.

lessons.title: Voters' list, nomination, campaign and polling

scenes.text: Meera shows her EPIC card at the polling booth. An official checks her name on the voters' list.
Indelible ink is marked on her finger. She presses a button on the EVM next to her chosen candidate's symbol.

steps.title: Voters' list
steps.body: In a democratic election, the list of eligible voters (the **electoral roll / voters' list**) is prepared well in advance. Every citizen aged **18 years and above** has the right to vote, regardless of caste, religion or gender (**universal adult franchise**). Some criminals and persons of unsound mind can be denied the vote in rare situations. The list is revised regularly. The government has introduced the **Election Photo Identity Card (EPIC)**; voters may show it or other approved IDs.

steps.title: Nomination of candidates
steps.body:
Anyone who can be a voter can also become a candidate; the minimum age for a candidate is **25 years** (for Lok Sabha and assemblies). Parties nominate their candidates who get the party symbol and support ('party ticket'). Every candidate fills a **nomination form** and pays a **security deposit**. Following a Supreme Court direction, every candidate must make a legal declaration giving details of:
- serious **criminal cases** pending against them
- **assets and liabilities** of the candidate and family
- **educational qualifications**

steps.title: Campaign, polling and counting
steps.body:
**Campaign**: usually about two weeks between the announcement of the final list of candidates and polling. Slogans like 'Garibi Hatao' (Congress, 1971), 'Save Democracy' (Janata Party, 1977), 'Land to the Tiller' (Left Front, West Bengal 1977), 'Protect the Self-Respect of the Telugus' (N.T. Rama Rao, TDP, 1983).
Laws forbid parties or candidates to: bribe or threaten voters; appeal on the basis of caste or religion; use government resources; spend beyond a limit. The **Model Code of Conduct**: no use of places of worship for propaganda; no use of government vehicles, aircraft and officials; once elections are announced ministers cannot lay foundation stones, take big policy decisions or make promises of public facilities.
**Polling**: voters go to polling booths; **Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs)** record votes, with a **VVPAT** slip for verification.
**Counting**: EVMs are secured; agents of all candidates are present; the candidate who secures the highest number of votes is declared elected (**first-past-the-post**).

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Why must candidates declare criminal cases and assets? (2 marks)** So voters can make an informed choice about who they are electing.

**Q2. Name any three things the Model Code of Conduct forbids. (3 marks)** Using places of worship for propaganda; using government vehicles or officials for campaigning; ministers laying foundation stones or announcing big decisions after elections are announced.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Voting age is **18**; candidate minimum age for Lok Sabha/assembly is **25**.
- 'Garibi Hatao' was Indira Gandhi's Congress slogan of **1971**, not 1977.
- The winner needs the **most** votes, not necessarily more than 50%.

activity.prompt: Order the stages of an election
items: Voters' list prepared and updated
Election dates announced
Candidates file nominations and declarations
Election campaign
Polling on EVMs
Counting and declaration of results

quiz.q: Minimum voting age in India:
quiz.why: The minimum voting age in India is 18 years, after it was lowered from 21 in 1988. Every citizen aged 18 or more can vote.

quiz.q: EPIC stands for:
quiz.why: EPIC stands for Election Photo Identity Card, which voters may show at the polling booth as proof of identity.

quiz.q: 'Garibi Hatao' was the slogan of:
quiz.why: 'Garibi Hatao' was the slogan of the Congress under Indira Gandhi in the 1971 Lok Sabha elections. Other parties used different slogans.

quiz.q: Candidates must declare:
quiz.why: Following Supreme Court direction, candidates must declare their criminal cases, assets and liabilities, and educational qualifications. This helps voters make an informed choice.

quiz.q: Which is forbidden under the Model Code of Conduct?
quiz.why: The Model Code of Conduct bars the ruling party from using government vehicles or resources for campaigning. Door-to-door campaigns, public meetings and manifestos are allowed.

lessons.title: What makes elections in India democratic?

scenes.text: Mrs D'Souza, a school teacher, is posted as a presiding officer in a remote village. On election duty she works under the Election Commission, not her school.
She carries the EVMs on foot across a river. Every vote matters, she says.

steps.title: Independent Election Commission
steps.body:
Elections in India are conducted by an independent and very powerful **Election Commission (EC)**, which enjoys independence similar to the judiciary. The **Chief Election Commissioner (CEC)** is appointed by the **President of India**; once appointed, the CEC is not answerable to the President or the government.
Powers of the EC:
- Takes decisions on every aspect of conduct and control of elections, from announcement to declaration of results.
- Implements the **Code of Conduct** and punishes violators.
- During elections, can order the government to follow guidelines to prevent misuse of power, or transfer officials.
- Government officers on election duty work under the EC's control.

steps.title: Popular participation and acceptance
steps.body:
- **Voter turnout** in India has remained stable or gone up; in India, the poor, illiterate and underprivileged vote in larger proportion compared to the rich and privileged (opposite of Western democracies).
- Common people attach great importance to elections — they can bring pressure on parties.
- Interest in election-related activities is growing.
- **Acceptance of results**: ruling parties often lose elections at national and state levels ('**anti-incumbency**'); about half of sitting MPs or MLAs lose; candidates who spend much money and have criminal links often lose; results are generally accepted as the 'people's verdict'.

steps.title: Challenges to free and fair elections
steps.body:
- Candidates and parties with a lot of money may have an unfair advantage.
- In some parts, candidates with criminal connections have been able to push others out.
- Some families tend to dominate political parties; tickets go to relatives.
- Very often elections offer little choice to ordinary citizens as major parties are similar in policies and practice.
- Smaller parties and independents suffer a huge disadvantage compared to bigger parties.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Give three reasons the EC is considered independent and powerful. (3 marks)** CEC not answerable to the government once appointed; controls all officers on election duty; can enforce the Code of Conduct and transfer officials.

**Q2. Why do 'the poor vote more' in India? (2 marks)** They see elections as a means to bring their concerns to the attention of parties and to influence policies.

a.text: A week before polling, a candidate's worker offers your family ₹2,000 to vote for his candidate.

choices.label: Accept the money quietly
choices.feedback: Bribing voters is an electoral offence and undermines fair elections.

choices.label: Refuse and report it to the Election Commission's helpline/cVIGIL app
choices.feedback: Reporting helps keep elections free and fair.

b.text: Your neighbour, who refused, asks: 'Will the winner listen to us after buying our votes?'

choices.label: Realise the mistake and report future offers

c.text: The EC's flying squad acts on complaints. On polling day you vote for the candidate you genuinely prefer.

quiz.q: The Chief Election Commissioner is appointed by:
quiz.why: The Chief Election Commissioner is appointed by the President of India. Once appointed, he or she is independent of the government.

quiz.q: In India, who votes in larger proportion?
quiz.why: In India the poor and underprivileged vote in larger proportion than the rich, unlike in many Western democracies where the rich vote more.

quiz.q: 'Anti-incumbency' means:
quiz.why: Anti-incumbency means that ruling parties often lose elections, as voters vote them out. It shows that elections are competitive.

quiz.q: During elections, officers on election duty work under:
quiz.why: During election time, the officers on election duty work under the Election Commission, not the government. This helps keep the election fair.

quiz.q: Which is a challenge to fair elections?
quiz.why: Money and muscle power give rich and criminal candidates an unfair edge, which challenges fair elections. EVMs, universal franchise and an independent EC support fairness.

questions.q: Voting age in India:
questions.why: The voting age in India is 18 years. The age was 21 until it was lowered in 1988.

questions.q: Elections in India are conducted by:
questions.why: Elections in India are conducted by the independent Election Commission. Parliament, courts and the police do not run them.

questions.q: Number of Lok Sabha constituencies:
questions.why: The Lok Sabha has 543 elected constituencies, each sending one member. 545 earlier included two nominated members.

questions.q: In a reserved constituency, who can contest?
options: Only members of the reserved group
questions.why: In a reserved constituency, only members of the reserved group (SC or ST) can contest, though all voters in the area vote.

questions.q: Minimum age to contest Lok Sabha elections:
questions.why: The minimum age to contest Lok Sabha elections is 25, while the voting age is 18.

questions.q: 'Land to the Tiller' was a slogan of:
questions.why: 'Land to the Tiller' was the slogan of the Left Front in West Bengal, which won in 1977 and carried out land reform.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Indian elections are largely free and fair. Reason (R): An independent Election Commission conducts them.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. Indian elections are largely free and fair mainly because an independent Election Commission conducts them. So the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Case: After elections are announced, a minister plans to inaugurate a new bridge to win votes. What applies?
options: Model Code of Conduct forbids it
Only Supreme Court can stop it
questions.why: After elections are announced, the Model Code of Conduct forbids ministers from announcing or inaugurating new projects. This stops the ruling party from gaining an unfair advantage.

questions.q: Which is NOT required in a candidate's declaration?
questions.why: Candidates must declare criminal cases, assets and liabilities and educational qualifications. A caste certificate of all relatives is not required.

questions.q: What shows that Indian elections are competitive?
questions.why: When ruling parties often lose elections, it shows real competition. If the same party always won, elections would not be competitive.

questions.q: A constituency has 4 candidates getting 35%, 30%, 25%, 10%. Who wins under first-past-the-post?
options: The top two share the seat
questions.why: In first-past-the-post, the candidate with the highest number of votes wins, even without 50%. So the one with 35% wins.

questions.q: If 84 SC and 47 ST seats are reserved out of 543, what percentage is reserved in total?
questions.why: Reserved seats = 84 + 47 = 131. 131 ÷ 543 × 100 ≈ 24%. Add the SC and ST seats first, then divide by the total.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Political competition is wholly harmful. Reason (R): It can create factionalism.
questions.why: The assertion is false because competition also gives an incentive to serve people. The reason is true, since it can create factionalism, so only R is correct.

questions.q: Case: A district collector, during elections, ignores EC instructions on the ruling party's request. What can the EC do?
options: Order his transfer and ensure officials work under EC control
questions.why: The EC controls officials on election duty, so it can order the transfer of an officer who ignores its instructions. It cannot cancel all elections or dismiss the government.

questions.q: Which best explains the purpose of reserved constituencies?
options: To ensure weaker sections are represented despite disadvantages in open competition
questions.why: Reserved constituencies ensure that weaker sections get represented, since they may be disadvantaged in open competition. They do not give extra votes or exclude others.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Working of Institutions
courses.summary: How a major policy decision is taken, and how Parliament, the political executive (President, PM, Council of Ministers) and the judiciary work and check each other.
outcomes: Learners can trace how a major policy decision (the Mandal Commission case) was taken
Learners can explain the need for and powers of Parliament and its two Houses
Learners can distinguish political and permanent executives and describe the PM and President
Learners can explain the independence and powers of the judiciary, including judicial review and PIL

lessons.title: How is a major policy decision taken?

scenes.text: 13 August 1990: an Office Memorandum is signed by a Joint Secretary in the Department of Personnel and Training.
It announces 27% reservation for socially and educationally backward classes in central government jobs. The country erupts in debate.

steps.title: The Mandal Commission story
steps.body:
- The **Second Backward Classes Commission**, headed by **B.P. Mandal**, was appointed in **1979**; it is popularly called the **Mandal Commission**. It gave its report in **1980**, recommending **27%** of government jobs be reserved for the socially and educationally backward classes (SEBC).
- The **Janata Dal** promised implementation in its 1989 Lok Sabha manifesto. After the elections, **V.P. Singh** became Prime Minister.
- The **President**, in his address to Parliament, announced the intention; on **6 August 1990** the Union Cabinet formally decided.
- The PM informed both Houses; the decision was sent to the **Department of Personnel and Training**, whose senior officers drafted an order. An **Office Memorandum** (O.M. No. 36012/31/90-Est (SCT)) dated **13 August 1990** was signed by the Joint Secretary.
- Widespread protests and counter-protests followed. Cases were filed in the courts — known as the **'Indira Sawhney and others vs Union of India'** case. In **1992**, the **Supreme Court** declared the order valid, but asked the government to modify it so that well-to-do persons among backward classes ('**creamy layer**') would be excluded.

steps.title: Need for political institutions
steps.body:
Governing a country involves many activities: security, education, health, taxes, welfare. Democracies arrange for **institutions**:
- **Prime Minister and Cabinet** take important policy decisions.
- **Civil servants** implement them.
- **Supreme Court** settles disputes between citizens and government.
Institutions involve rules and regulations that may cause delays, but they also provide opportunities for a wider set of people to be consulted — which is good for democracy.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Name the institutions involved in the 1990 reservation decision. (3 marks)** President (announced), Union Cabinet and PM (decided), Parliament (informed and debated), civil servants of DoPT (drafted order), Supreme Court (reviewed).

**Q2. What did the Supreme Court decide in the Indira Sawhney case? (2 marks)** The order was valid, but the creamy layer among backward classes had to be excluded.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The Mandal Commission was appointed in **1979**, reported in **1980**, implemented by O.M. in **1990**, upheld in **1992**.
- The O.M. was **signed by a Joint Secretary**, not the PM.
- Reservation is **27%** for SEBC.

activity.prompt: Order the Mandal decision

events.text: Supreme Court upholds with creamy layer exclusion

quiz.q: The Mandal Commission was headed by:
quiz.why: The Mandal Commission was headed by B.P. Mandal and studied the condition of the socially and educationally backward classes. Indira Sawhney was the petitioner in a later case.

quiz.q: Reservation recommended for SEBC:
quiz.why: The Mandal Commission recommended 27% reservation in government jobs for the Socially and Educationally Backward Classes (SEBC).

quiz.q: The O.M. was dated:
quiz.why: The Office Memorandum announcing 27% reservation for backward classes was issued on 13 August 1990.

quiz.q: The famous case on this order:
options: Indira Sawhney vs Union of India
quiz.why: The Supreme Court heard the challenge to the Mandal order in the Indira Sawhney and others vs Union of India case. Kesavananda Bharati and Golaknath were other cases.

quiz.q: The Supreme Court asked the government to exclude:
quiz.why: The Supreme Court asked the government to exclude the creamy layer, meaning the well-off persons among the backward classes, from the benefit of reservation.

scenes.text: In the Lok Sabha, an MP asks the Railway Minister why a train accident happened.
The minister must answer. Asking questions is one way Parliament controls the government.

steps.title: Why Parliament?
steps.body:
In all democracies, an assembly of elected representatives exercises supreme political authority on behalf of the people. In India it is called **Parliament**; at state level, the **Legislature** or **Legislative Assembly**.
Parliament:
1. Is the **final authority for making laws**; it can make new laws, change existing ones or abolish them.
2. **Exercises control** over those who run the government — the government can take decisions only so long as it enjoys the support of Parliament.
3. **Controls all the money** that governments have — public money can be spent only when Parliament sanctions it.
4. Is the **highest forum of discussion and debate** on public issues and national policy.

steps.title: Two Houses
steps.body:
India's Parliament has two Houses (bicameral) and the President.
- **Lok Sabha (House of the People)**: directly elected by the people; exercises real power on behalf of the people.
- **Rajya Sabha (Council of States)**: indirectly elected; looks after the interests of states and regions.

The **Lok Sabha is more powerful**:
1. Any ordinary law needs both Houses; if there is a difference, a **joint session** decides — Lok Sabha's larger numbers usually prevail.
2. In **money matters**, Lok Sabha has more power: once it passes the budget or any money bill, the Rajya Sabha cannot reject it; it can only **delay it by 14 days** or suggest changes, which the Lok Sabha may or may not accept.
3. Lok Sabha **controls the Council of Ministers**: only a person who enjoys the support of the majority in the Lok Sabha is appointed PM; if a majority says it has 'no confidence', the PM and ministers must quit. Rajya Sabha has no such power.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Give two reasons the Lok Sabha is more powerful. (2 marks)** Final say on money bills (Rajya Sabha can delay only 14 days); a no-confidence vote in Lok Sabha removes the government.

**Q2. What happens when the two Houses disagree on an ordinary bill? (2 marks)** A joint session is held; because the Lok Sabha has more members, its view usually prevails.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The Rajya Sabha can delay a money bill by **14 days**, not 14 months.
- Rajya Sabha members are **indirectly** elected (by state MLAs).
- Only the **Lok Sabha** can pass a no-confidence motion.

activity.prompt: Which House?

items.text: Can delay a money bill only 14 days

quiz.q: Which House is directly elected?
quiz.why: Members of the Lok Sabha are directly elected by the people. Rajya Sabha members are elected indirectly by state legislators.

quiz.q: The Rajya Sabha can delay a money bill by:
quiz.why: The Rajya Sabha can delay a money bill by only 14 days. The Lok Sabha then has the final say.

quiz.q: If the Houses disagree on an ordinary bill:
quiz.why: If the two Houses disagree on an ordinary bill, a joint session of Parliament is held, where the larger Lok Sabha usually prevails.

quiz.q: Who can remove the Council of Ministers by a no-confidence vote?
quiz.why: The Council of Ministers is answerable to the Lok Sabha, which can remove it by a no-confidence vote. The Rajya Sabha cannot.

quiz.q: Public money can be spent only with sanction of:
quiz.why: Public money can be spent only with the sanction of Parliament. This control over finance is a key power of Parliament.

lessons.title: Political executive: PM, Council of Ministers and President

scenes.text: The new Health Minister, a doctor-turned-politician, is elected for five years.
Her Health Secretary, a senior IAS officer, has served for 25 years. Who decides, and who advises?

steps.title: Political vs permanent executive
steps.body:
The **executive** is the body that takes day-to-day decisions and implements them.
- **Political executive**: elected by the people for a specific period — political leaders who take the big decisions (PM, ministers).
- **Permanent executive**: appointed on a long-term basis — civil servants; they remain in office even when the ruling party changes.
Why does the political executive have more power? In a democracy the will of the people is supreme; the minister is elected and answerable to the people. The minister decides the overall framework and objectives; civil servants, who have expertise, advise and implement.

steps.title: Prime Minister and Council of Ministers
steps.body:
- The **President appoints** the leader of the majority party or coalition that commands a majority in the Lok Sabha as **Prime Minister**. The PM has no fixed tenure; continues as long as he/she remains leader of the majority.
- The President appoints other ministers on the PM's advice; ministers must be members of Parliament (a non-member must become one within **six months**).
- **Council of Ministers** (usually 60–80 ministers) has three ranks:
  - **Cabinet Ministers** — top-level leaders in charge of major ministries (about 25); the **Cabinet** is the inner ring.
  - **Ministers of State with independent charge** — in charge of smaller ministries.
  - **Ministers of State** — attached to and assist Cabinet Ministers.
- The Cabinet works as a team: **collective responsibility** — every minister owns up to every decision of the Cabinet.
- Powers of the PM: chairs Cabinet meetings, coordinates departments, distributes and redistributes work, can dismiss ministers; when the PM quits, the entire ministry quits.

steps.title: The President
steps.body: The **President** is the **head of the State**, a nominal executive who exercises powers mostly on the advice of the Council of Ministers. Elected **indirectly** by an electoral college of elected MPs and elected MLAs. All governmental activities take place in the President's name; all laws and major policy decisions are issued in his/her name; major appointments (Chief Justice, judges, Governors, Election Commissioners, ambassadors) are made in his/her name. The President is the **supreme commander** of the defence forces. The President can ask the Council of Ministers to reconsider advice once; but if the same advice is sent again, the President is bound to act on it. A bill passed by Parliament becomes a law only after the President gives assent. The President has discretion in appointing a PM when no party has a clear majority.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Why does a minister have more power than a civil servant? (2 marks)** The minister is elected and represents the people's will; the civil servant is appointed to advise and implement.

**Q2. What is collective responsibility? (2 marks)** All ministers are jointly responsible to the Lok Sabha for Cabinet decisions; no minister can openly criticise a Cabinet decision.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The President is **indirectly** elected; the PM is **appointed** by the President, not directly elected.
- The PM has **no fixed tenure**.
- Civil servants are the **permanent** executive.

activity.prompt: Match the office with its feature
pairs: Nominal head of State, indirectly elected
Head of government; leader of Lok Sabha majority
Heads a major ministry; in the inner ring

quiz.q: The President of India is elected by:
quiz.why: The President is elected indirectly by an electoral college of elected MPs and MLAs. There is no direct popular vote.

quiz.q: A minister who is not an MP must become one within:
quiz.why: A person who is not an MP can be made a minister, but must become a member of Parliament within six months.

quiz.q: Collective responsibility means:
options: All ministers own Cabinet decisions jointly
quiz.why: Collective responsibility means all ministers jointly own the decisions of the Cabinet. If one minister loses confidence, the whole ministry is affected.

quiz.q: Civil servants are part of the:
quiz.why: Civil servants are appointed for a long tenure and remain in office even when the government changes, so they are part of the permanent executive.

quiz.q: If the PM resigns:
quiz.why: If the Prime Minister resigns, the entire ministry quits, because the Council of Ministers works under the PM. Parliament is not automatically dissolved.

scenes.text: A group of citizens write to the Supreme Court about children working in dangerous factories.
The court treats it as a Public Interest Litigation and orders the government to act.

steps.title: Structure and independence
steps.body:
India has an **integrated judiciary**: the **Supreme Court** for the entire nation, **High Courts** in the states, **District Courts** and courts at the local level.
- The Supreme Court controls judicial administration; its decisions are binding on all other courts.
- It can hear disputes between citizens, between citizens and government, between states, and between the Union and states. It is the highest court of appeal in civil and criminal cases.

**Independence**: the judiciary is not under the control of the legislature or executive; judges do not act on the government's direction.
- Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts are appointed by the **President** on the advice of the PM and in consultation with the **Chief Justice of India** (in practice, senior judges — the collegium — select new judges).
- A judge can be removed only by an **impeachment motion** passed separately by **two-thirds** members of the two Houses of Parliament — it has never happened in Indian history.

steps.title: Powers
steps.body:
- **Judicial review**: the Supreme Court and High Courts can declare invalid any law of the legislature or action of the executive (Union or state) if it is against the Constitution.
- **Basic structure**: the Supreme Court has ruled that the core or **basic principles of the Constitution cannot be changed** by Parliament.
- **Guardian of Fundamental Rights**: citizens can approach the courts if their rights are violated.
- **Public Interest Litigation (PIL)**: anyone can approach the courts if public interest is hurt by government action; courts intervene to prevent misuse of power and check malpractices.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. How is the independence of the judiciary ensured? (3 marks)** Judges appointed with the Chief Justice's consultation, not by politicians alone; removal only by two-thirds impeachment in both Houses (very difficult); decisions not controlled by the executive.

**Q2. What is PIL? (2 marks)** A case filed in court by any person or group on behalf of the public to protect public interest.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Judicial review checks laws against the **Constitution**, not against public opinion.
- Impeachment needs **two-thirds** in **each** House separately.
- District courts are part of the same integrated system — India doesn't have separate state and federal judiciaries like the USA.

statements.s: The Supreme Court can declare a law unconstitutional.
A Supreme Court judge can be removed by the PM.
Any citizen can file a PIL on a public issue.
Parliament can change the basic structure of the Constitution.
statements.why: The Supreme Court has ruled it cannot.

quiz.q: Judges of the Supreme Court are appointed by:
options: The President, in consultation with the Chief Justice
quiz.why: Supreme Court judges are appointed by the President in consultation with the Chief Justice. The PM alone, the EC or Lok Sabha do not appoint them.

quiz.q: Removal of a judge requires:
quiz.why: A judge can be removed only by impeachment, which needs a two-thirds majority in each House of Parliament. This protects judicial independence.

quiz.q: The power to examine the constitutional validity of laws:
quiz.why: Judicial review is the power of the courts to examine the constitutional validity of laws. A veto is a power to reject a bill, and an ordinance is a temporary law.

quiz.q: India's judiciary is:
quiz.why: India has an integrated judiciary, with the Supreme Court at the top and High Courts and lower courts under it. Its judges are not elected.

quiz.q: PIL stands for:
quiz.why: PIL stands for Public Interest Litigation, which allows any person to go to court on behalf of those whose rights are affected.

questions.q: The head of the State in India:
questions.why: The President is the head of the State in India, while the Prime Minister is the head of government. The Chief Justice heads the judiciary.

questions.q: The highest court of India:
questions.why: The Supreme Court is the highest court of India. High Courts and District Courts are below it.

questions.q: Which House represents the states?
questions.why: The Rajya Sabha, or Council of States, represents the states of India. The Lok Sabha represents the people.

questions.q: The Mandal Commission report was submitted in:
questions.why: The Mandal Commission submitted its report in 1980. The order for implementing it was issued in 1990.

questions.q: Who appoints the PM?
questions.why: The President appoints the Prime Minister, usually the leader of the party or coalition with a majority in the Lok Sabha.

questions.q: Permanent executive refers to:
questions.why: The permanent executive means the civil servants, who stay in office as governments change. Ministers form the political executive.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Lok Sabha is more powerful than Rajya Sabha in money matters. Reason (R): Rajya Sabha can only delay a money bill by 14 days.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. The Rajya Sabha can only delay a money bill by 14 days, so the Lok Sabha has the final say in money matters. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Case: The President returns the Cabinet's advice for reconsideration; the Cabinet sends the same advice back. What must the President do?
questions.why: The President can return the Cabinet's advice once for reconsideration, but if the Cabinet sends it back again, the President must act on it.

questions.q: Which is the correct order of ranks in the Council of Ministers (highest first)?
questions.why: The Council of Ministers has three ranks, from highest to lowest: Cabinet ministers, Ministers of State with independent charge, and Ministers of State.

questions.q: Which institution decided the Indira Sawhney case?
questions.why: The Supreme Court decided the Indira Sawhney case in 1992. Courts, not Parliament or the Cabinet, settle such disputes.

questions.q: A joint session has 543 Lok Sabha and 245 Rajya Sabha members. If all Lok Sabha members and 45 Rajya Sabha members vote for a bill, will it pass by simple majority of all 788?
questions.why: Total votes for = 543 + 45 = 588. Half of 788 is 394, and 588 is more than 394, so the bill passes by a simple majority.

questions.q: For impeachment, if 540 Lok Sabha members are present and voting, at least how many must support?
questions.why: Two-thirds of 540 = 360, so at least 360 members must support it. Impeachment also needs a majority of the total membership.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The Prime Minister has a fixed five-year term. Reason (R): The PM continues as long as he/she has majority support in the Lok Sabha.
questions.why: The assertion is false because the PM does not have a fixed term. The reason is true: the PM continues as long as he or she has the support of a majority in the Lok Sabha.

questions.q: Case: A state law bans a community from buying land, violating equality. Citizens go to the High Court. Which power will the court use?
questions.why: Courts use judicial review to strike down laws that violate the Constitution. A law that breaks the equality right would be struck down by the High Court.

questions.q: Why are institutions valuable despite causing delays?
options: They allow wider consultation and prevent hasty, arbitrary decisions
questions.why: Institutions involve wider consultation and prevent hasty or arbitrary decisions, even though they may cause delays. This is good for democracy.

courses.title: Ch 5 · Democratic Rights
courses.summary: Life without rights, what rights are and why democracy needs them, the six Fundamental Rights in India, how they are protected, and the expanding scope of rights.
outcomes: Learners can explain what rights are and why they matter, using cases like Guantanamo, Saudi Arabia and Kosovo
Learners can describe the six Fundamental Rights
Learners can explain the Right to Constitutional Remedies and the role of NHRC
Learners can describe new and expanding rights

lessons.title: Life without rights; what are rights?

scenes.text: A man is picked up in one country and taken to a prison on a foreign base. His family is not told where he is.
He is never brought before a judge. Years pass. Without rights, he has no one to turn to.

steps.title: Three cases of life without rights
steps.body:
- **Prison in Guantanamo Bay**: about 600 people were secretly picked up by US forces from all over the world and put in a prison at Guantanamo Bay (an area near Cuba controlled by the American Navy). Families were not informed; they were not tried before any magistrate in the US, nor could they approach courts. **Amnesty International** reported that prisoners were being treated in ways that violated US laws and international treaties. Even the UN Secretary General said the prison should be closed; the US government refused.
- **Citizens' rights in Saudi Arabia**: the country is ruled by a hereditary king; people have no role in electing or changing rulers; no freedom of religion for non-Muslim public worship; women are subjected to many public restrictions (they got the vote in local elections in 2015).
- **Ethnic massacre in Kosovo**: a province of the former Yugoslavia where ethnic Albanians were the majority. Under the nationalist **Milosevic**, the Serb-dominated forces carried out massacres of Albanians. Several other countries intervened (NATO) to stop it. Milosevic was later tried by an International Court of Justice for crimes against humanity.

steps.title: What are rights?
steps.body:
**Rights** are **reasonable claims** of persons recognised by society and sanctioned by law. They are claims of a person over other fellow beings, over society and over the government. Claims must be reasonable — what I claim for myself, I must also accept for others. A right becomes enforceable when written into law. When our rights are violated, we can seek remedy from the courts.

Rights are necessary for democracy: citizens must have the right to vote, express opinions, form parties. Rights protect **minorities** from oppression by the majority; they guarantee that the majority cannot do whatever it likes. Rights act as guarantees when things go wrong — even governments may attack citizens' rights, so some rights are placed higher than the government.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Define rights. (2 marks)** Reasonable claims of persons, recognised by society and sanctioned by law.

**Q2. Why do we need rights in a democracy? (3 marks)** Every citizen needs them to vote and contest; they protect minorities from majority tyranny; they guard against governments violating citizens' freedoms.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- A demand is not a right until **society recognises** it and **law sanctions** it.
- Rights come with the duty to respect others' rights.

activity.prompt: Match the case to the rights violation
pairs: Detention without trial or access to courts
No say in choosing rulers; restrictions on religion and women

quiz.q: Guantanamo Bay prison was run by:
quiz.why: The Guantanamo Bay prison was run by the US Navy, on land in Cuba, where prisoners were held without trial. It was not run by Cuba or the UN.

quiz.q: In Kosovo, the massacres targeted:
quiz.why: In Kosovo, a province of Yugoslavia, the massacres targeted ethnic Albanians, who were the majority there. It shows how rights can be violated.

quiz.q: Milosevic was tried for:
quiz.why: Milosevic, the Serbian president, was tried by an international court for crimes against humanity, including the massacre of Kosovo Albanians.

quiz.q: Rights are claims that are:
quiz.why: Rights are reasonable claims of a person that are recognised by society and sanctioned by law. They are not only for the rich or just moral demands.

quiz.q: Rights protect minorities from:
quiz.why: Rights protect minorities from the oppression of the majority, as the majority cannot do whatever it likes. This is one purpose of rights.

lessons.title: Fundamental Rights I: Equality and Freedom

story.title: A temple door and a tea stall

scenes.text: A Dalit boy is told he cannot enter a public well area or sit with others at a tea stall.
His teacher explains: untouchability is abolished by the Constitution. Practising it is a punishable offence.

steps.title: Right to Equality
steps.body:
- The government shall not deny to any person in India **equality before the law** or the **equal protection of the laws** — **rule of law**: no person is above the law; there is no distinction between a political leader, government official and an ordinary citizen.
- No discrimination on grounds of **religion, caste, ethnicity, sex or place of birth** in access to public places: shops, restaurants, hotels, cinemas, wells, tanks, bathing ghats, roads, playgrounds.
- **Equality of opportunity** in public employment; reservations for SC, ST and OBC (and EWS) are not a violation, but a means to substantive equality.
- **Untouchability abolished** (Article 17) in any form; it is a punishable offence.

steps.title: Right to Freedom
steps.body:
Under the Constitution, all citizens have the right to:
- Freedom of **speech and expression**
- **Assembly** in a peaceful manner
- Form **associations and unions**
- **Move freely** throughout the country
- **Reside** in any part of the country
- Practise any **profession**, or carry on any occupation, trade or business
These are subject to **reasonable restrictions** (public order, security, decency, etc.).

**Right to life and personal liberty** (Article 21): no person can be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. A person arrested must be informed of the reasons, produced before the nearest magistrate within **24 hours**, and has the right to talk to a lawyer.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Name four freedoms under the Right to Freedom. (2 marks)** Speech and expression; peaceful assembly; forming associations; moving and residing anywhere; practising any profession.

**Q2. What rights does an arrested person have? (3 marks)** To be told the reasons for arrest; to be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours; to consult a lawyer.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Freedom of speech is not absolute — it has **reasonable restrictions**.
- Reservations do **not** violate the right to equality.
- 24 hours (excluding travel time) — not 48.

activity.prompt: Right to Equality or Right to Freedom?

items.text: A restaurant cannot refuse entry because of caste
A citizen of Kerala can settle in Punjab
A minister is equal before the law
A journalist writes criticism of the government

quiz.q: Untouchability was abolished by:
quiz.why: Article 17 abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form. Article 14 is about equality before law, Article 21 about life, and Article 32 about remedies.

quiz.q: An arrested person must be produced before a magistrate within:
quiz.why: An arrested person must be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours. This protects against illegal detention.

quiz.q: Rule of law means:
options: No one is above the law
quiz.why: Rule of law means no one is above the law, not even the ruler or officials. Everyone is equal before it.

quiz.q: Freedoms under Article 19 are subject to:
quiz.why: The freedoms in Article 19 are subject to reasonable restrictions, such as those for public order. They are not unlimited.

quiz.q: Do reservations violate the Right to Equality?
quiz.why: Reservations do not violate the Right to Equality. They are special measures to promote substantive equality for disadvantaged groups.

lessons.title: Fundamental Rights II: Exploitation, Religion, Culture, Remedies

scenes.text: Eleven-year-old Raju works 12 hours a day weaving carpets to pay off his father's debt.
A neighbour calls Childline 1098. Raju is rescued and admitted to school — the Constitution forbids such exploitation.

steps.title: Right against Exploitation
steps.body:
The Constitution prohibits:
1. **Traffic in human beings** (selling and buying of humans, usually women, for immoral purposes).
2. **Forced labour (begar)** in any form — work without remuneration; when a worker is forced to work for a master for life because of a debt, it is **bonded labour**.
3. **Child labour**: no child below **14 years** can be employed in any factory, mine or other hazardous work such as railways and ports.
Laws such as the bonded labour abolition law and child labour laws enforce these.

steps.title: Freedom of Religion; Cultural and Educational Rights
steps.body:
**Freedom of Religion**: India is **secular**. Every person has a right to profess, practise and propagate the religion he or she believes in. Every religious group is free to manage its religious affairs. The government cannot compel anyone to pay taxes to promote a particular religion. No religious instruction in government educational institutions; in private educational institutions, no one can be compelled to take part in religious instruction or worship.

**Cultural and Educational Rights**: any section of citizens with a distinct **language or culture** has a right to conserve it; admission to a government or government-aided educational institution cannot be denied on grounds of religion or language; **all minorities** have the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice.

steps.title: Right to Constitutional Remedies
steps.body:
This is the right to seek remedy if any Fundamental Right is violated. A citizen can go directly to the **Supreme Court or a High Court**. The courts can issue directions, orders or **writs**. Dr **Ambedkar** called it the **'heart and soul'** of the Constitution.
- Any law or action of the government that violates Fundamental Rights is invalid.
- In case of violation, the victim can approach courts; in public interest matters, anyone can (**PIL**).
- **National Human Rights Commission (NHRC)**: an independent commission set up by law in **1993**. It focuses on helping victims secure their rights; it cannot punish the guilty itself but can conduct independent inquiries, visit jails and custody, and make recommendations to the government or intervene in courts. Anyone can write to the NHRC; no fee.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Why is the Right to Constitutional Remedies called the heart and soul of the Constitution? (3 marks)** It makes all other rights effective — without it, rights could be violated with no remedy; courts can enforce rights against the government itself.

**Q2. What three things does the Right against Exploitation prohibit? (3 marks)** Human trafficking; forced/bonded labour; employment of children below 14 in hazardous work.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- NHRC **cannot punish** — it inquires and recommends.
- Right to Property is **not** a Fundamental Right now (removed in 1978; now a constitutional right under Article 300A).
- The 'heart and soul' quote is by **Ambedkar** about the right to constitutional remedies.

activity.prompt: Match the Fundamental Right to the situation
pairs: Rescue of a child from a hazardous factory
A minority runs its own school
Going to the Supreme Court when rights are violated
No discrimination at a public well

quiz.q: Children below what age cannot be employed in hazardous work?
quiz.why: Children below 14 years cannot be employed in hazardous work such as factories or mines. This protects children under the right against exploitation.

quiz.q: Ambedkar called which right the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution?
quiz.why: Dr Ambedkar called the Right to Constitutional Remedies the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution because it lets citizens enforce all other rights in court.

quiz.q: The NHRC was set up in:
quiz.why: The National Human Rights Commission was set up in 1993 to look into human rights violations.

quiz.q: Can the NHRC punish the guilty?
quiz.why: The NHRC cannot punish the guilty. It can inquire into violations and make recommendations to the government or courts.

quiz.q: How many Fundamental Rights are there now?
quiz.why: There are six Fundamental Rights now. The right to property was removed from the list, leaving six.

scenes.text: Sunita's ration card application is stuck for months. She files an RTI application asking for the status.
Within weeks, her card is issued. The Right to Information made officials accountable.

steps.title: New rights
steps.body:
The scope of rights has expanded over time; courts have interpreted existing rights to include new ones.
- **Right to Education**: under **Article 21A** (added 2002) and the **Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009**, children aged **6–14** have a right to free and compulsory education.
- **Right to Information**: the **RTI Act, 2005** lets citizens seek information from government offices (Supreme Court earlier held it part of freedom of expression).
- **Right to life** has been expanded by courts to include the **right to food**, **right to livelihood** and the **right to privacy** (Supreme Court, 2017).
- **Right to property**: no longer a Fundamental Right (since the **44th Amendment, 1978**) but a constitutional right — the government cannot take property except by law and with compensation.
- Constitutional rights also include the right to vote in elections (a **constitutional right**, not a Fundamental Right).
- Human rights frameworks: the **International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights** recognises rights to work, safe working conditions, adequate standard of living (food, clothing, housing), social security, health and education. South Africa's constitution guarantees rights to privacy, adequate housing, health care, sufficient food and water.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Name two new rights that have expanded the scope of rights in India. (2 marks)** Right to Information (2005); Right to Education for 6–14 year olds (2009 Act).

**Q2. Is the right to property a Fundamental Right? (2 marks)** No; it was removed in 1978 and is now a constitutional right under Article 300A.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- RTI Act = **2005**; RTE Act = **2009**.
- Right to vote is a **constitutional/legal** right, not a Fundamental Right.

steps.title: Using RTI
steps.body: An RTI application is written to the Public Information Officer of a department, with a small fee (waived for BPL applicants). The office must generally reply within **30 days**.

statements.s: The RTI Act was passed in 2005.
statements.why: It lets citizens seek government information.

statements.s: Children aged 6–14 have a right to free and compulsory education.
The right to property is a Fundamental Right today.
Courts have held privacy to be part of the right to life.

quiz.q: The RTE Act covers children aged:
quiz.why: The Right to Education Act covers children aged 6 to 14, providing free and compulsory education.

quiz.q: The RTI Act was enacted in:
quiz.why: The Right to Information Act was enacted in 2005, letting citizens seek information from government offices.

quiz.q: The right to property was removed from Fundamental Rights by the:
quiz.why: The right to property was removed from the Fundamental Rights by the 44th Amendment in 1978. It is now a legal right.

quiz.q: Which right have courts read into the right to life?
quiz.why: Courts have read the right to privacy as part of the right to life and liberty, as the Supreme Court held in 2017. The other options are not rights.

quiz.q: The right to vote is a:
quiz.why: The right to vote is a constitutional right, not a Fundamental Right. It is given by the Constitution and electoral laws.

questions.q: How many Fundamental Rights are there?
questions.why: There are six Fundamental Rights: equality, freedom, against exploitation, freedom of religion, cultural and educational rights, and constitutional remedies.

questions.q: Article 17 deals with:
questions.why: Article 17 deals with the abolition of untouchability. Right to life is Article 21.

questions.q: The NHRC was set up in:
questions.why: The National Human Rights Commission was set up in 1993.

questions.q: Which is NOT a Fundamental Right?
questions.why: The right to property is no longer a Fundamental Right because it was removed by the 44th Amendment. The other three are among the six.

questions.q: Rights are claims that are:
options: Reasonable, recognised by society and sanctioned by law
questions.why: Rights are reasonable claims, recognised by society and sanctioned by law. Not every demand is a right.

questions.q: The prison at Guantanamo Bay is associated with:
questions.why: The prison at Guantanamo Bay is associated with detention without trial, as prisoners were denied access to courts. It has nothing to do with elections or reform.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Fundamental Rights can be enforced against the government. Reason (R): The Right to Constitutional Remedies lets citizens approach the Supreme Court directly.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. Fundamental Rights can be enforced against the government because citizens can approach the Supreme Court directly under the Right to Constitutional Remedies. So R explains A.

questions.q: Case: A government school requires all students to attend a prayer of one religion. Which right is violated?
questions.why: Forcing all students to attend the prayer of one religion in a government school violates the freedom of religion, since no one can be compelled to take part in religious instruction.

questions.q: Case: A brick-kiln owner forces a family to work without wages to repay a loan. This is:
questions.why: Forcing a family to work without wages to repay a loan is bonded labour, a form of forced labour banned under the right against exploitation.

questions.q: A minority community starts its own college. Which right supports this?
questions.why: Cultural and Educational Rights let minorities set up and run their own educational institutions to protect their culture.

questions.q: Which right is a Fundamental Right AND has been expanded by courts to include food and livelihood?
options: Right to life and personal liberty
questions.why: The right to life and personal liberty (Article 21) is a Fundamental Right that courts have read broadly to include food and livelihood. The right to information is not a Fundamental Right.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Freedom of speech in India is absolute. Reason (R): It is subject to reasonable restrictions like public order.
questions.why: The assertion is false because freedom of speech is not absolute. The reason is true, since it is subject to reasonable restrictions such as public order, so only R is correct.

questions.q: An RTI reply must generally come within 30 days. If applied on 5 March, the last date is about:
questions.why: 30 days from 5 March: March has 31 days, so 26 days remain after 5 March, and 4 more days give 4 April. 5 March + 30 days = 4 April.

questions.q: Case: Police detain a student for 3 days without producing her before a magistrate. Which remedy fits best?
options: Approach the High Court/Supreme Court for violation of Article 21 rights
questions.why: Detaining her for 3 days without producing her before a magistrate breaks the 24-hour rule. She can approach the High Court or Supreme Court for violation of her Article 21 rights.

questions.q: Why do rights protect minorities in a democracy?
options: Rights are placed above ordinary majority decisions, so the majority cannot take them away
questions.why: Rights are placed above ordinary majority decisions, so the majority cannot take them away. This is how rights protect minorities.
